entries.title: crate — a compiled unit of Rust code
entries.l1: A crate is one buildable chunk of Rust — think of it like a single npm package or a .csproj project. This codebase is split into several: `graph-types` (the shared vocabulary of nodes and edges), `atlas-core`, `atlas-etl`, `atlas-graph`, `atlas-server`, `atlas-cli`. Each compiles on its own and can depend on others. If `graph-types` vanished, nothing else could even describe what a Place or a verse IS — every other crate imports its types.
entries.l3: This workspace has six crates: `graph-types` (root-level, deliberately NOT a Cargo workspace member — see `workspace`), and `atlas-core`, `atlas-etl`, `atlas-graph`, `atlas-server`, `atlas-cli` under `server/`. `graph-types/src/lib.rs:16-26` is the library root, declaring its modules and re-exporting the small `covenant` surface (`lib.rs:35-40`) that the sibling map-system project is allowed to depend on — everything else in the crate can change without notice. `atlas-graph` depends on `graph-types` via a plain path dependency (`server/atlas-graph/Cargo.toml`), which is what pulls a non-member crate into one shared `Cargo.lock` (see `workspace`). Crate boundaries here are also API boundaries: crossing one always means going through `pub` items only.

entries.title: module — folders and files as namespaces
entries.l1: A module is Rust's way of organizing code into named drawers, like folders or packages elsewhere. `mod id;` in a crate's entry file says 'there's a drawer called id, defined in id.rs' — that's how a 2,000-line crate stays navigable instead of one giant file. Modules also control what's visible from outside (see `visibility`): put something in a module and don't mark it `pub`, and no other file can reach it, keeping internal helpers internal.
entries.l3: `graph-types/src/lib.rs:16-26` declares eleven top-level modules (`id`, `text`, `node`, `edge`, `chrono`, `ingest`, `graph`, `explore`, `frontier`, `present`, `store`); `lib.rs:73` also has an inline `mod tests;` for the crate's own law tests. Modules nest arbitrarily (`graph-types/src/id.rs` has an inner `#[cfg(test)] mod tests` too, at the bottom of files like `graph.rs:514-515`). Module boundaries here roughly track the domain: `id.rs` owns identity, `edge.rs` owns relations, `store.rs` owns the query contract (`GraphQuery` trait). A privacy nuance worth knowing: `pub(crate)` (used in `server/atlas-core/src/data.rs:2019`, `server/atlas-cli/src/commands/find.rs:30-31`) makes an item visible everywhere in ITS crate but invisible outside it — narrower than `pub`, wider than private.

entries.title: struct — a named bundle of fields
entries.l1: A struct groups related pieces of data under one name, the way a spreadsheet row groups columns. `Graph` bundles every node and every kind of edge the app knows about; a `Place` struct would bundle a name, a position, maybe a modern-day label. If structs vanished, you'd have no way to hand around 'a place' as one thing — you'd be passing five separate loose values everywhere and hoping they stay in sync.
entries.l2:
Declare fields with `struct Name { field: Type, ... }` (a 'named-field' struct) or `struct Name(Type, ...)` (a 'tuple' struct — see `newtype`). Fields are private by default; add `pub` per field or on the struct to expose them.

Example:
```
pub struct Graph {
    pub nodes: BTreeMap<AnyNodeId, Node>,
    pub attests: Vec<Attests>,
}
```
Newcomer mistake: expecting a struct to have methods baked in like a class. Rust separates data (the `struct`) from behavior (a separate `impl` block) — see `impl`.
entries.l3: `graph-types/src/graph.rs:25-27` — `pub struct Graph { pub nodes: BTreeMap<AnyNodeId, Node>, ... }` — is the crate's central data structure; every other field below it (`contains_bible`, `attests`, `succession`, etc., `graph.rs:29-34`) is one typed edge relation stored as a flat `Vec`. Structs here are also used as zero-field 'tag' markers (`graph-types/src/id.rs:38-39`, generated by the `kind_tags!` macro) purely to carry a type through generics — see `phantom-type`. `#[derive(...)]` on a struct (see `derive`) is how most of them get `Debug`, `Clone`, `PartialEq`, etc. for free rather than hand-written.

entries.title: enum — one of several named shapes
entries.l1: An enum lists every shape a value is allowed to take — like a multiple-choice question where the compiler checks you've handled every option. `NodeKind` is 'Place, Person, Event, Era, Polity, ...and nothing else' — the closed vocabulary of things the graph can hold. This matters for honesty: if the codebase invented a new kind of node without updating the enum and every place that switches on it, the compiler refuses to build until you've dealt with the new case.
entries.l2:
`enum Name { VariantA, VariantB(Type), VariantC { field: Type } }` — variants can carry no data, a tuple of data, or named fields, unlike enums in most other mainstream languages. You inspect which variant you have with `match` (see `match`) or `if let`.

Example:
```
pub enum NodeKind {
    Place,
    Person,
    Event,
    // ...
}
```
Newcomer mistake: treating an enum like a C-style int flag. Rust enums are 'sum types' — each variant can carry its OWN different payload, which is what makes `Option` and `Result` (both enums under the hood) possible.
entries.l3: `graph-types/src/id.rs:13-29` — `pub enum NodeKind` — is explicitly called a 'closed node-kind vocabulary' whose doc comment (`id.rs:9-12`) says extending it is 'a deliberate act every exhaustive match must acknowledge': adding a variant breaks every non-wildcard `match` on `NodeKind` until it's handled, by design. `RelationId`/`SymRelationId` in `graph-types/src/edge.rs` are enums generated by the `relations!` macro (`edge.rs:42`) and matched exhaustively at `edge.rs:25,56,59,66` to compute each relation's forward/inverse/symmetric kind. Error types are also enums: `CoreError` (`server/atlas-core/src/lib.rs:20-31`) has one variant per failure mode, each carrying its own payload (e.g. `Io { path: String, source: std::io::Error }`).

entries.title: trait — a promised set of methods
entries.l1: A trait is a promise: 'any type that implements me supports these operations.' It's Rust's version of an interface. `GraphQuery` is the promise the rest of the app makes about how it will ask questions of the graph — 'give me this node', 'how many edges of each kind leave here', 'the next twenty verses'. Any storage that can keep that promise can sit underneath the app, which is what lets the project swap its storage later without touching the reader or the map.
entries.l3: `graph-types/src/store.rs`'s `GraphQuery` trait (per this codebase's own design note) declares five methods — `node`, `derive`, `edge_summary`, `edges`, `reading_window` — and `Graph` implements it, which the crate's own tests enforce as a 'canonical instance' law (every other backend's answers must match the in-memory graph's). `KindTag` (`graph-types/src/id.rs:33-36`) is a trait with only an associated `const`, used purely to carry compile-time identity through `NodeId<K>` — see `phantom-type`. `pipeline.rs` uses a trait as an interface for build-pipeline passes: `Vec<Box<dyn Pass>>` (`server/atlas-graph/src/pipeline.rs:549,565`) is a runtime-dispatched list of heterogeneous pass implementations — see `Box`.

entries.title: impl — where a type's behavior lives
entries.l1: An `impl` block is where you write the functions that belong to a struct or enum — its methods. Data (the struct) and behavior (the impl block) are declared separately in Rust, unlike a class in most other languages where they're one unit. `impl Graph { ... }` is where you'd find 'how do I look up a node', separate from the `struct Graph` that says what a Graph HOLDS.
entries.l3: `graph-types/src/id.rs:68-75` — `impl<K: KindTag> NodeId<K>` — attaches `new` and `erase` to every kind-tagged id type at once, generic over the tag `K` (see `generics`, `trait-bound`). Trait impls are pervasive: `impl std::fmt::Display for ArtifactError` (`server/atlas-graph/src/artifact.rs:65`) gives a custom error type a human-readable message; `impl KindTag for $tag { const KIND = ...; }` (`graph-types/src/id.rs:41`) is generated fourteen times by the `kind_tags!` macro rather than hand-written. The distinction to keep straight: an inherent `impl Type` block's methods are only callable when the type is known; a trait `impl Trait for Type` block's methods are callable through the trait too (`dyn Trait`, or a generic `T: Trait`).

entries.title: generics — write it once, for any type
entries.l1: Generics let you write one function or struct that works for many types instead of copy-pasting it per type — like a shipping container that works whether it holds books or bricks, without the shipping company caring which. `NodeId<K>` is one definition that becomes 'a Place id', 'a Person id', 'an Event id', etc. depending on what `K` is filled in with, instead of thirteen near-identical hand-written id types.
entries.l2:
Angle brackets after a name introduce a generic parameter: `struct NodeId<K>`, `fn first<T>(items: &[T]) -> Option<&T>`. Usually paired with a trait bound (see `trait-bound`) restricting which types are allowed.

Example:
```
pub struct NodeId<K: KindTag>(pub Interned, pub PhantomData<K>);
```
Here `K` isn't stored as data at runtime at all — see `phantom-type`; it exists purely so the compiler can tell a `NodeId<PlaceTag>` and a `NodeId<PersonTag>` apart. Newcomer mistake: assuming generics work like Java/C# generics with runtime type info available — Rust generics are compiled away per concrete type (monomorphization), so there's no `typeof(K)` at runtime unless the trait itself exposes one (as `KindTag::KIND` does).
entries.l3: `graph-types/src/id.rs:67` (`pub struct NodeId<K: KindTag>`) is this codebase's flagship generic type: a phantom-typed id where the type parameter exists only to make 'comparing a Place id to a Person id' a compile error rather than a runtime bug (id.rs:32-33's own doc comment: 'a cross-kind reference is a type error, not a runtime surprise'). `corpus_key<C: Corpus>() -> &'static str` (`graph-types/src/graph.rs:510`) is a smaller generic function bounded by the `Corpus` trait. Monomorphization means each concrete instantiation (`NodeId<PlaceTag>`, `NodeId<PersonTag>`, ...) is compiled as its own type with zero runtime overhead versus a hand-written non-generic version — the phantom type costs nothing at runtime.

entries.title: trait-bound — generics with a requirement
entries.l1: A trait bound is the fine print on a generic: 'this works for any type T, AS LONG AS T can do these specific things.' Without a bound, a generic function can't call any methods on its placeholder type at all — the compiler has no idea what it can do. `K: KindTag` on `NodeId<K>` says 'K must be one of the recognized node-kind tags', which is what lets `NodeId::new` read `K::KIND` to know which kind of id it's building.
entries.l3: `graph-types/src/id.rs:67-68`: `NodeId<K: KindTag>` and its `impl<K: KindTag> NodeId<K>` block both carry the bound, letting `erase()` (id.rs:72-74) call `K::KIND` to build an `AnyNodeId`. `pub fn new(raw: impl Into<Interned>) -> Self` (id.rs:70) is an argument-position trait bound (`impl Trait` sugar for a bound generic parameter) — see `From-Into`. `corpus_key<C: Corpus>()` (`graph-types/src/graph.rs:510`) bounds by the `Corpus` trait to read `C::ID`. Trait bounds are how this codebase gets compile-time guarantees (a `NodeId<PlaceTag>` provably has a `NodeKind`) without runtime type-checking or reflection.

entries.title: lifetime — how long a reference is good for
entries.l1: A lifetime is the compiler's way of making sure you never hold onto a reference to something after it's gone — like a library card that stops working the moment the book is returned. You never invent the actual duration; you just tell the compiler two references are tied together ('this returned reference is only valid as long as that input is'), and it verifies you never break that promise.
entries.l2:
Written as `'a` (an apostrophe plus a name, usually a single letter). `fn f<'a>(x: &'a str) -> &'a str` means: the returned reference lives exactly as long as `x` does.

Example:
```
fn one_positional<'a>(rest: &'a [String], cmd: &str, shape: &str)
    -> Result<&'a str, CliError> { ... }
```
Here the returned `&'a str` borrows from `rest`, so the compiler forbids using the result after `rest` is dropped. Newcomer mistake: trying to 'fix' a lifetime error by adding `'a` everywhere at random. Lifetimes describe existing relationships between references; they don't create new ones — if the error persists, the actual fix is usually to return an owned value (`String` instead of `&str`) instead.
entries.l3: `server/atlas-cli/src/main.rs:229` (`fn one_positional<'a>(rest: &'a [String], ...) -> Result<&'a str, CliError>`) ties the returned string slice's lifetime to the input slice's. `server/atlas-core/src/translation.rs:37,49` (`resolve<'a>`, `resolve_name<'a>`) do the same for translation lookups, and `server/atlas-core/src/chronology.rs:406` (`window_for_book<'a>(...) -> Option<&'a BookNarrationWindow>`) returns a borrowed `Option`. Most of this codebase's data-carrying types (`Graph`, `NodeId`) own their data instead of borrowing it, so explicit lifetimes cluster in small lookup functions rather than throughout — a sign of a codebase that mostly avoids the added complexity of borrowed long-lived structures in favor of owned `String`/`Vec` data (see `String-vs-str`, `ownership`).

entries.title: ownership — exactly one owner at a time
entries.l1: Rust's core idea: every value has exactly one owner, and when that owner goes away, the value is cleaned up automatically — no garbage collector guessing when, no manual free. Hand a value to a function and you've handed over ownership (unless you explicitly lend a reference — see `borrowing`); the original owner can no longer use it. This is what lets Rust guarantee memory safety without a garbage collector pausing your program.
entries.l2:
Assigning or passing a non-`Copy` value moves it: `let a = String::from("x"); let b = a;` makes `a` unusable afterward — the compiler flags any later use of `a` as an error at compile time, not a runtime crash. Types that are cheap to duplicate (numbers, etc.) implement `Copy` instead and don't move — see `Clone-Copy`.

Example:
```
let raw: String = load_name();
let id = NodeId::<PlaceTag>::new(raw); // raw is moved in
```
Newcomer mistake: fighting ownership by cloning everything to make errors go away. That compiles, but it's usually a sign you should be borrowing (`&T`) instead of taking ownership.
entries.l3: `NodeId::new(raw: impl Into<Interned>)` (`graph-types/src/id.rs:70-71`) takes `raw` by value — it MOVES the caller's string in and owns it from then on, matching `Interned`'s status as an owned `String` type alias (id.rs:8). `Graph` (`graph-types/src/graph.rs:25-34`) owns every node and edge it holds — no field is a reference — which is a deliberate simplification this codebase's tests rely on: an owned graph in memory means no lifetime parameter threads through `GraphQuery` implementations, keeping the trait itself lifetime-free. The tradeoff, paid at load time, is that building the artifact clones/moves data rather than borrowing from a longer-lived source; see `content-hash` and `artifact.rs`'s `dump` for where that owned data gets serialized.

entries.title: borrowing — using without taking
entries.l1: Borrowing is asking to use a value without taking it away from its owner — like reading a book at the library instead of buying it. You get a reference (see `reference`); the owner keeps ownership and can lend it out to many readers at once, or to exactly one writer, but never both simultaneously. The compiler enforces that rule (the 'borrow checker') so two parts of the program can never quietly stomp on the same data at the same time.
entries.l2:
`&value` borrows for reading (any number of shared borrows can coexist); `&mut value` borrows for writing (only one at a time, and no shared borrows while it's alive).

Example:
```
fn edges(&self, at: Position) -> EdgeSummary { ... }
```
`&self` here borrows the graph immutably — calling this method doesn't consume the graph, so you can call it again right after. Newcomer mistake: trying to hold a `&mut` borrow and a `&` borrow of the same value at once ('cannot borrow as mutable because it is also borrowed as immutable') — the fix is almost always to shrink the borrow's scope, not to sprinkle `.clone()` everywhere.
entries.l3: Query methods across this codebase take `&self` (shared borrow) since reading the graph shouldn't require exclusive access — see the `GraphQuery` trait's methods (`graph-types/src/store.rs`). `std::thread::scope`'s parallel build path (`server/atlas-graph/src/artifact.rs:1430`, `graph-types/src/graph.rs:393-408`) is a case where borrowing rules do real safety work across threads: `graph.rs:112`'s doc comment calls it 'safe, unsafe-free data parallelism' — the borrow checker statically proves no two spawned threads can mutate the same data at once, which is exactly what would otherwise need a `Mutex` (see `Mutex`) or manual discipline in a language without borrow checking.

entries.title: reference — a pointer the compiler checks
entries.l1: A reference is an address pointing at a value someone else owns — like a hyperlink to a document rather than a photocopy of it. `&Graph` says 'here's where to find the graph, I'm not giving it to you.' Unlike a raw pointer in C, the compiler checks every reference to guarantee it never outlives the thing it points at and never gets used to write while someone else is reading — no dangling pointers, no data races, verified before the program ever runs.
entries.l2:
`&T` is a shared (read-only) reference; `&mut T` is an exclusive (read-write) reference. Dereference with `*r` when you need the value itself rather than the pointer to it (often unnecessary — method calls auto-dereference).

Example:
```
fn node(&self, id: &AnyNodeId) -> Option<&Node> { ... }
```
Both `&self` and `&AnyNodeId` are borrowed, and the returned `Option<&Node>` borrows FROM the graph too, so it can't outlive it. Newcomer mistake: confusing `&Type` (a reference to something owned elsewhere) with `Type` itself — passing a reference where an owned value is expected (or vice versa) is one of the most common early compile errors.
entries.l3: `graph-types/src/store.rs`'s `GraphQuery` methods take `&self` and reference parameters throughout, returning borrowed data tied to the graph's own lifetime. `server/atlas-cli/src/main.rs:229`'s `rest: &'a [String]` is a reference to a slice (see `slice`) of owned `String`s, borrowed rather than copied — passing potentially many command-line arguments around without duplicating them. This codebase generally prefers borrowing over cloning in hot lookup paths (queries) and owning in build/storage paths (`Graph`'s fields), a common Rust idiom: own data where it lives, borrow it where it's merely read.

entries.title: slice — a view into part of a sequence
entries.l1: A slice is a window onto a run of elements — 'these five items, starting here' — without copying them. Think of it like a crop of a photo: you're pointing at a region of the original image, not making a new one. `&[String]` is 'a borrowed view of some run of strings', which is how this codebase passes around command-line arguments or lists of ids without duplicating them every time a function wants to look at a few.
entries.l2:
`&[T]` (a shared slice) or `&mut [T]` (a mutable slice) — a pointer plus a length, tracked together so out-of-bounds access is caught rather than silently reading garbage memory. `&str` is specifically a slice of UTF-8 bytes (see `String-vs-str`).

Example:
```
fn one_positional<'a>(rest: &'a [String], cmd: &str, shape: &str)
    -> Result<&'a str, CliError> { ... }
```
`rest: &'a [String]` is a slice of the full argument `Vec<String>`, not a copy of it. Newcomer mistake: expecting `[T]` alone (no `&`) to be usable as a type in a variable — a bare `[T]` is 'unsized' (its length isn't known at compile time), so it can only ever be used behind a reference or a `Box`.
entries.l3: `server/atlas-cli/src/main.rs:229`'s `rest: &'a [String]` and `server/atlas-etl/src/red_letter.rs:138`'s `attr<'a>(tag: &'a str, ...)` both slice into caller-owned data rather than taking ownership. `&str` itself (used throughout, e.g. `translation.rs:49`'s `Result<&'a str, CoreError>`) is the slice-of-`String` case: a `String` owns a growable heap buffer, while `&str` borrows some run of it — that's the whole distinction covered under `String-vs-str`. Slices are why passing 'part of a Vec' around is cheap in Rust — no allocation, no copy, just a pointer and a length checked at every access.

entries.title: Option<T> — maybe a value
entries.l1: `Option<T>` is Rust's honest way of saying 'there might not be an answer.' Instead of a function silently returning `null` and letting you find out the hard way (a crash) when you use it, Rust makes 'nothing here' part of the type itself — you're FORCED to check before you can get at the value. Looking up a place by an id you made up gets you `None`, not a mysterious crash three steps later.
entries.l2:
`Option<T>` is an enum with two variants: `Some(value)` or `None`. You unwrap it safely with `match`, `if let Some(x) = opt { ... }`, or combinators like `.map()`, `.unwrap_or()`, `.ok_or()` (turns it into a `Result`).

Example:
```
pub fn window_for_book<'a>(windows: &'a [BookNarrationWindow], book: &str)
    -> Option<&'a BookNarrationWindow> {
    windows.iter().find(|w| w.book == book)
}
```
Newcomer mistake: calling `.unwrap()` on an `Option` you haven't proven is `Some` — that panics at runtime if it's `None`, which is exactly the crash `Option` exists to let you avoid. Reach for `.unwrap()` only in tests or when you've already checked.
entries.l3: `server/atlas-core/src/chronology.rs:406` (`window_for_book`) and `graph-types/src/store.rs`'s `node`/`derive` methods return `Option` for lookups that may legitimately miss. `graph-types/src/id.rs:135` returns `Result<Self, KindMismatch>` rather than `Option` when a MISMATCH (not merely an absence) is the failure — a deliberate distinction: `None` means 'not found', `Err` means 'found something, but it's wrong.' Combinators seen in this codebase include `.map()` and `?` via `ok_or`-style conversions at API boundaries (`server/atlas-server/src/graph_handlers.rs`) turning a missing node into a proper HTTP error rather than a panic.

entries.title: Result<T, E> — success or a named failure
entries.l1: `Result<T, E>` is how Rust functions say 'this might fail, and here's what failure looks like' as part of the return type — not as a separately-thrown exception you might forget to catch. Reading a data file might fail because the file's missing, or because its contents don't parse; `Result` forces the caller to decide what to do in both cases before the code compiles, rather than discovering it live when a file is missing in production.
entries.l2:
`Result<T, E>` is an enum: `Ok(value)` on success, `Err(error)` on failure. The `?` operator (see `?-operator`) is the idiomatic way to propagate an `Err` up to the caller without a manual `match` at every step.

Example:
```
pub fn resolve<'a>(translations: &'a HashMap<String, Vec<String>>, code: &str)
    -> Result<&'a [String], CoreError> {
    translations.get(code).map(Vec::as_slice)
        .ok_or_else(|| CoreError::UnknownCode(code.into()))
}
```
Newcomer mistake: using `Result<T, String>` everywhere for convenience. It compiles, but throws away the ability to `match` on WHICH failure happened — this codebase instead defines real error enums (see `error-handling`).
entries.l3: `server/atlas-core/src/translation.rs:37,49` return `Result<..., CoreError>`; `CoreError` (`server/atlas-core/src/lib.rs:20-31`) is a `thiserror`-derived enum with one variant per real failure mode (`Io`, `Json`, etc.), so callers can `match` on the exact cause. ETL parsing throughout `server/atlas-etl/src/compile.rs` returns `anyhow::Result` instead (see `anyhow`) — a deliberate difference: library crates (`atlas-core`) expose a precise, matchable error type, while the ETL binary's own top-level plumbing (`compile.rs:73-77`) just needs to propagate-and-report, for which `anyhow` is idiomatic. `Result` and `Option` interconvert via `.ok_or()`/`.ok()`.

entries.title: ? — propagate the error and stop
entries.l1: The `?` after a function call means 'if this failed, stop here and hand the failure up to whoever called me; otherwise, give me the successful value and keep going.' It replaces writing the same 'if it failed, return early' check by hand after every fallible step — one character does what would otherwise be several lines of boilerplate, and it can't accidentally be forgotten the way an unchecked error code can.
entries.l3: `server/atlas-etl/src/compile.rs:73-77` chains four `?`s in a row reading and parsing source files — any failure short-circuits the whole compile with that step's specific error. `server/atlas-server/src/bins/export_aqc_examples.rs:54` (`async fn main() -> anyhow::Result<()>`) is the pattern that lets `?` work directly in a binary's entry point. The error type produced by `?` must implement `From<OriginalError>` for the function's declared error type (usually satisfied automatically by `anyhow::Result`'s blanket conversion, or by `#[source]` fields in a `thiserror` enum like `CoreError`) — see `From-Into` and `error-handling`.

entries.title: match — branch on every possible shape
entries.l1: `match` is a switch statement that the compiler holds to a higher standard: you must account for every possibility, or it won't compile. Given a `NodeKind`, a `match` covering Place, Person, and Event but forgetting Era is a compile error, not a silent bug waiting to surface the day someone visits an Era. It's how this codebase enforces 'when we add a new kind of thing, every place that reacts to kinds must be updated.'
entries.l3: `graph-types/src/edge.rs:25,56,59,66` all `match self { ... }` over `RelationId`/`SymRelationId` to compute forward/inverse/symmetric relation kinds — generated by the `relations!` macro so each new relation is added in exactly one place, with the macro expanding it into every needed `match` arm. `graph-types/src/edge.rs:126` matches on `NodeKind` (`match k { ... }`). Because `NodeKind` (`graph-types/src/id.rs:13-29`) is explicitly documented as a closed vocabulary, its doc comment (id.rs:11) calls out that adding a variant requires 'every exhaustive match' to acknowledge it — the compiler enforces that promise for free.

entries.title: pattern-matching — taking values apart by shape
entries.l1: Pattern matching is the ability to say 'if this value looks like THIS shape, pull out THESE pieces' in one step — like sorting mail by both envelope color and what's printed on it, extracting the sender's name only from the ones that match. `Ok(value)` isn't just a check that a `Result` succeeded; the pattern also names `value` for you to use immediately, no separate unwrap step.
entries.l2:
Patterns appear in `match` arms, `if let`, `let` bindings, and function parameters. They can destructure structs, enums, tuples, and nest arbitrarily.

Example:
```
Err(KindMismatch { expected: K::KIND, found: self.kind })
```
This both matches the `Err` variant AND destructures a `KindMismatch` struct's fields by name in one pattern. Newcomer mistake: writing `if x == Some(5)` instead of `if let Some(5) = x` — the latter is idiomatic pattern matching and reads more naturally once it clicks, and is required at all once the thing you're comparing isn't `PartialEq`.
entries.l3: `graph-types/src/id.rs:135` (`Err(KindMismatch { expected: K::KIND, found: self.kind })`) constructs — the mirror-image use, pattern-matching's underlying machinery, would destructure it the same way on the receiving end. Macro-generated code leans on patterns heavily: `kind_tags!` (`graph-types/src/id.rs:40-46`) and `relations!` (`graph-types/src/edge.rs:42`) both use `$(...)` repetition patterns to expand a compact table into many `match` arms and `impl` blocks — patterns aren't only for consuming values, they're also central to how `macro_rules!` itself is written.

entries.title: if let — match just the case you care about
entries.l1: `if let` is a shortcut for when you only care about ONE shape a value might have and want to ignore the rest — 'if this happens to be a Some, do something with it; otherwise, move on' — without writing a full `match` with an empty catch-all arm. It reads almost like plain English once you've seen it a few times.
entries.l3: `graph-types/src/store.rs:248` (`if let Some(n) = &b { ... }`) is this codebase's example: checking one branch of an `Option` inline rather than a full `match`. This idiom is common wherever a lookup's success case matters but the absence case is a plain no-op or an early return — it keeps the 'happy path' code visually flat instead of nested inside a `match` arm.

entries.title: closure — a function that remembers its surroundings
entries.l1: A closure is a small, on-the-spot function that can reach out and use variables from the code around it — like a sticky note you write that still remembers what desk it came from. `.map(|chunk| ...)` hands a mini-function to `.map()` that processes each chunk; that mini-function is a closure, and it can see `scope` and other nearby variables without you passing them in explicitly.
entries.l2:
`|params| expression` or `|params| { block }`. Closures capture their environment by reference, by mutable reference, or by move (`move |params| ...`), depending on what the body needs.

Example:
```
chunk.iter().map(|(_, n)| (n.pid(), n.id.clone()))
    .collect::<BTreeMap<_, _>>()
```
The closure `|(_, n)| ...` destructures a tuple parameter (see `pattern-matching`) and builds a new tuple per element. Newcomer mistake: fighting a `move` closure that 'stole' a variable you wanted to keep using afterward — `move` transfers ownership into the closure (see `ownership`), so clone beforehand if you need the original too.
entries.l3: `graph-types/src/graph.rs:408` — `.map(|chunk| scope.spawn(move || chunk.iter().map(|(_, n)| (n.pid(), n.id.clone())).collect::<BTreeMap<_, _>>()))` — nests THREE closures: an outer one building spawn tasks, a `move` closure handed to `thread::scope` (see `scoped-threads`) that owns its chunk, and an inner one used by `.map()` on the chunk's iterator. The `move` there is required because each closure must own its slice of work independently once handed to a separate thread — sharing a borrow across threads would violate the same rules `borrowing` describes, just checked across a `thread::scope` boundary instead of a single function.

entries.title: iterator — a recipe for producing values one at a time
entries.l1: An iterator is a lazy recipe for 'give me the next item' repeated until there are none left — like a conveyor belt that only moves when you ask for the next piece, rather than dumping everything on you at once. `.iter().map(...).collect()` reads as a pipeline: look at each item, transform it, then gather the results — and nothing actually runs until `.collect()` (or similar) asks for the output.
entries.l2:
Any type implementing the `Iterator` trait (with a `next()` method) can be chained with `.map()`, `.filter()`, `.find()`, `.collect()`, and dozens more adapters, all without allocating an intermediate list at each step.

Example:
```
windows.iter().find(|w| w.book == book)
```
finds the first matching window without building a temporary filtered list. Newcomer mistake: calling `.collect()` after every intermediate step 'just to see it' — that defeats the laziness and allocates memory you didn't need; chain the adapters and collect once at the end.
entries.l3: `graph-types/src/graph.rs:408` chains `.iter().map(...).collect::<BTreeMap<_,_>>()` to build a lookup table from a chunk of nodes. `server/atlas-core/src/chronology.rs:406`'s `window_for_book` uses `.iter().find(...)` for a linear scan. This codebase generally favors iterator chains over hand-written index loops for anything that reads, filters, or transforms a collection — partly for concision, partly because it composes cleanly with `.collect::<BTreeMap<_, _>>()`/`.collect::<Vec<_>>()` when the exact deterministic container matters (see `sort-determinism`).

entries.title: Vec<T> — a growable list
entries.l1: `Vec<T>` is Rust's resizable array — a list that can grow as you push items onto it, like an ArrayList or a Python list. It's the default 'give me an ordered bunch of things' container. `Graph`'s `attests: Vec<Attests>` is literally the flat list of every attestation edge in the graph, in the order they were added.
entries.l2:
`Vec::new()` or the `vec![]` macro to build one; `.push()` to append; index with `v[i]` (panics if out of bounds) or `v.get(i)` (returns `Option`, see `Option`, for safe access).

Example:
```
pub struct ReadingSpine {
    pub order: Vec<AnyNodeId>, // canonical order of materialized units
}
```
Newcomer mistake: reaching for `Vec` when order doesn't matter and duplicates shouldn't be allowed — `BTreeSet`/`HashMap` often model the actual requirement (a set, a lookup table) more honestly than a `Vec` you then have to de-duplicate by hand.
entries.l3: `graph-types/src/graph.rs:29-34` stores every edge relation as a plain `Vec` (`contains_bible: Vec<Contains<BibleTag>>`, `attests: Vec<Attests>`, `succession: Vec<Succession>`, ...) — flat row tables, deliberately not indexed, mirroring how the artifact is eventually dumped as row-oriented bytes (`artifact.rs`'s `dump`). `server/atlas-graph/tests/determinism.rs:13-15` explicitly credits this Vec-based, never-HashMap-keyed design for the artifact's byte-for-byte reproducibility — see `sort-determinism`. `Vec<Box<dyn Pass>>` (`server/atlas-graph/src/pipeline.rs:549`) is a `Vec` of trait objects, an ordered, heterogeneous pipeline.

entries.title: HashMap<K,V> — fast lookup, unordered
entries.l1: `HashMap<K, V>` is a lookup table: give it a key, get back its value, fast, regardless of how many entries it holds — like a dictionary or a phone book indexed by name instead of page number. The tradeoff this codebase cares about a lot: iterating a `HashMap` visits entries in an essentially random order that can even change between runs of the SAME program, which is fine for lookups but dangerous if you serialize the iteration order to disk.
entries.l2:
`HashMap::new()`, `.insert(k, v)`, `.get(&k) -> Option<&V>`. Keys must implement `Hash` and `Eq`.

Example:
```
pub translations: HashMap<String, Vec<String>>,
```
Newcomer mistake: relying on `HashMap` iteration order for anything that gets written to disk, hashed, or compared byte-for-byte — Rust's `HashMap` deliberately randomizes its hash seed per process for security (DoS resistance), so that 'accidental' ordering isn't even stable run-to-run. If order matters, use `BTreeMap` instead — see `sort-determinism`.
entries.l3: `server/atlas-core/src/data.rs:545,762,1022-1023,1051` uses `HashMap<String, ...>` for translation tables, verse-by-reference and cross-reference lookups, and place histories — pure by-key lookup, never serialized in iteration order directly. `server/atlas-graph/tests/determinism.rs:8-15`'s own header comment names exactly this class of bug it fixed: the OLD `verses-kjv.json`/`cross-refs.json` writers were `HashMap`-keyed JSON dumps whose random per-process iteration order produced byte-different (though content-identical) files on every run; those writers were deleted, and everything the serialized graph artifact dumps now sources from `Vec`/`BTreeMap` fields instead (see `BTreeMap`).

entries.title: BTreeMap<K,V> — lookup with a guaranteed order
entries.l1: `BTreeMap<K, V>` is a lookup table like `HashMap`, but it keeps its keys sorted and always iterates in that same sorted order — like a card catalog filed alphabetically instead of a pile sorted by whatever order cards were added. Slightly slower per lookup than a `HashMap`, but iterating it twice, or on two different machines, always visits entries in the exact same order — which matters enormously when the result gets hashed or written to a file that must be byte-identical every time.
entries.l3: `graph-types/src/graph.rs:27` — `pub nodes: BTreeMap<AnyNodeId, Node>` — is the graph's primary node table, chosen specifically so that dumping the graph to bytes (`server/atlas-graph/src/artifact.rs`'s `dump`) produces the same output every time given the same input, which `server/atlas-graph/tests/determinism.rs` asserts directly by building the artifact twice and comparing bytes. `graph-types/src/explore.rs:46` (`type EdgeSummary = BTreeMap<EdgeKind, usize>`) and `graph-types/src/edge.rs:553-554` (`fwd`/`inv` adjacency maps) use the same pattern for the same reason: anything that ends up in a hash or a file needs `BTreeMap`, never `HashMap`.

entries.title: BTreeSet<T> — a sorted set with no duplicates
entries.l1: `BTreeSet<T>` holds a collection of unique values, sorted, with no duplicates possible — like a sorted, de-duplicated guest list. Add the same name twice and it only appears once; iterate it and you always get the same order. It's the 'just the unique, sorted items' counterpart to `BTreeMap`'s 'unique, sorted keys with values attached.'
entries.l2:
`BTreeSet::new()`, `.insert(v)` (returns `false` if already present), `.contains(&v)`. Elements must implement `Ord`.

Example:
```
pub struct Holdings(pub BTreeSet<Position>);
```
Newcomer mistake: reaching for a `Vec` plus manual de-duplication logic (`if !v.contains(&x) { v.push(x) }`) where a `BTreeSet` would give you uniqueness and order for free, more clearly and more efficiently for larger collections.
entries.l3: `graph-types/src/edge.rs:155` (`pub grounds: BTreeSet<Ground>`) and `graph-types/src/edge.rs:259` (`let distinct: BTreeSet<_> = chain.iter().collect();`) both use `BTreeSet` to deduplicate while keeping deterministic order. `graph-types/src/explore.rs:149` (`pub struct Holdings(pub BTreeSet<Position>)`) wraps one in a newtype (see `newtype`) representing 'the distinct positions someone is holding/viewing.' Like `BTreeMap`, the choice over `HashSet` here is deliberate for determinism, not accidental — the same law that governs `BTreeMap` applies.

entries.title: String vs &str — owned text vs. borrowed text
entries.l1: Rust splits 'text' into two types on purpose: `String` is text you own — you can grow it, change it, and it lives until you're done with it, like a notebook page you can keep writing on. `&str` is a borrowed VIEW of text someone else owns — like reading a sentence someone else wrote, useful but not yours to keep or edit. Function parameters usually take `&str` (cheap to pass, works with either kind of text); return values or struct fields that need to own their data use `String`.
entries.l2:
`String::from("x")` or `"x".to_string()` to own text; `&str` (or a string literal `"x"`, which is already a `&str`) to borrow it. `String` derefs to `&str`, so you can call `&str` methods directly on a `String`.

Example:
```
pub type Interned = String; // owned
fn resolve_name<'a>(names: &'a HashMap<String, String>, code: &str)
    -> Result<&'a str, CoreError> // borrowed in, borrowed out
```
Newcomer mistake: writing `fn f(s: String)` for a parameter that only reads the text — that forces every caller to either own a `String` already or clone one; `fn f(s: &str)` accepts both a `&String` and a string literal with no extra cost.
entries.l3: `graph-types/src/id.rs:8` (`pub type Interned = String;`) commits ids to owned text — the crate's own doc comment (`lib.rs:11`) calls this a deliberate 'skeleton' simplification standing in for a future interner (see `interning`). Lookup functions borrow instead: `server/atlas-core/src/translation.rs:37,49` take `code: &str` and return `&'a str`/`&'a [String]` slices into the caller's own map, never allocating a new `String` just to answer a lookup. The rule of thumb this codebase follows: own text where it's stored long-term (ids, node payloads); borrow it (`&str`) where it's merely read or compared.

entries.title: Box<T> — a value on the heap, one owner
entries.l1: `Box<T>` puts a value on the heap instead of directly inline, and hands you a single owning pointer to it — useful when a value is too big to move around cheaply, or when you don't know its exact type ahead of time and only know it fulfills some trait. `Box<dyn Pass>` means 'some build-pipeline step, I don't need to know exactly which kind, just that it can run as a Pass.'
entries.l2:
`Box::new(value)` allocates and owns it; `Box<dyn Trait>` is a 'trait object' — a box holding ANY type that implements `Trait`, resolved at runtime rather than compile time (opposite of a generic's compile-time monomorphization — see `generics`).

Example:
```
pub fn pipeline() -> Vec<Box<dyn Pass>> {
    vec![Box::new(SomeStep), Box::new(AnotherStep)]
}
```
Newcomer mistake: reaching for `Box<dyn Trait>` where a plain generic (`fn f<T: Trait>(x: T)`) would do — a trait object costs a small runtime dispatch overhead and forbids some optimizations; use it specifically when you need a heterogeneous COLLECTION of different implementers, as the pipeline does.
entries.l3: `server/atlas-graph/src/pipeline.rs:549` (`pub fn pipeline() -> Vec<Box<dyn Pass>>`) is exactly that case: the build pipeline is an ORDERED LIST of heterogeneous passes, each a different concrete type, unified only by implementing the `Pass` trait — the pipeline.rs doc comment (line 4) calls passes 'DATA', formalizing the pipeline as 'an ordered contract.' `run_pipeline(ctx: &mut BuildCtx, passes: &[Box<dyn Pass>])` (pipeline.rs:565) then iterates that list generically, calling each pass without caring which concrete step it is. Tests filter and rebuild the list (pipeline.rs:595, 614) to check ordering and failure behavior.

entries.title: Arc<T> — shared ownership across threads
entries.l1: `Arc<T>` ('atomically reference-counted') lets multiple owners share the SAME value safely, even across threads — like several people holding the same library card that only gets returned once everyone's done with it. The library tracks how many people are holding it and doesn't shelve it until the count hits zero. It's the standard way this server hands the same loaded graph to every incoming web request without copying gigabytes of data per request.
entries.l2:
`Arc::new(value)` wraps it; `.clone()` on an `Arc` doesn't copy the underlying data — it just bumps a shared counter and hands out another pointer to the same value. Read-only sharing across threads is `Arc`'s specialty; for shared MUTATION you'd normally pair it with a `Mutex` or `RwLock`.

Example:
```
pub struct Loaded {
    pub graph: Arc<GraphService>,
    pub data: Arc<AtlasData>,
}
```
Newcomer mistake: assuming `Arc<T>` alone lets you mutate `T` from multiple threads — it doesn't; `Arc` only makes SHARING safe, not MUTATING. You still need interior mutability (`Mutex`/`RwLock`) for that, which this codebase doesn't need because its shared graph never changes after load.
entries.l3: `server/atlas-cli/src/load.rs:22-23` (`pub graph: Arc<GraphService>, pub data: Arc<AtlasData>`) and `server/atlas-server/benches/queries.rs:65` (`fn load_real() -> (Arc<AtlasData>, Arc<GraphService>)`) share one loaded, immutable graph across every request handler and every benchmark iteration without reloading or copying it. Notably, nothing in this codebase pairs `Arc` with a `Mutex` or `RwLock` (neither appears anywhere in `server/` or `graph-types/`) — because the graph is built once at startup and never mutated afterward, plain `Arc` is enough; there's no shared mutable state to protect.

entries.title: Rc<T> — shared ownership, single-threaded
entries.l1: `Rc<T>` ('reference-counted') is `Arc`'s single-threaded sibling: several owners share one value, and it's freed once the last owner drops it — but WITHOUT the extra bookkeeping `Arc` needs to stay safe across threads, so it's a little cheaper when you know everything stays on one thread. This codebase doesn't use it anywhere it was searched for.
entries.l2:
`Rc::new(value)`, `.clone()` bumps a plain (non-atomic) counter. The compiler refuses to let an `Rc` cross a thread boundary — trying to send one to another thread is a compile error, which is exactly the safety `Arc`'s extra cost buys back.

Example (illustrative, not from this repo):
```
use std::rc::Rc;
let shared = Rc::new(vec![1, 2, 3]);
let other_owner = shared.clone(); // same data, +1 to the count
```
Newcomer mistake: using `Rc` inside code that later gets moved to a multithreaded context (like an `async` handler that might run on any worker thread) — the compiler will reject it, and the fix is switching to `Arc`.
entries.l3: No use of `Rc` was found anywhere in `server/` or `graph-types/` (searched across all `.rs` sources). This tracks with the codebase's shape: shared data here (`GraphService`, `AtlasData`) is shared ACROSS an async web server's worker threads, so `Arc` (server/atlas-cli/src/load.rs:22-23) is the only sharing primitive needed — `Rc` would be a compile error the moment that data reached a `tokio` task on a different thread. It's documented here because a Rust newcomer will meet `Rc` immediately in tutorials and should know why THIS codebase skips it.

entries.title: Mutex<T> — one writer at a time
entries.l1: A `Mutex` ('mutual exclusion') is a lock: only one piece of code can hold it open and touch the data inside at a time; everyone else waits their turn. It's how you safely let multiple threads take turns MODIFYING the same shared data, where `Arc` alone only lets them safely SHARE read access. This codebase's search across `server/` and `graph-types/` found no use of `Mutex` anywhere.
entries.l3: No `Mutex` usage appears in this codebase's Rust sources. The reason follows directly from the architecture: `GraphService`/`AtlasData` are built once at startup and shared read-only via `Arc` (`server/atlas-cli/src/load.rs:22-23`) — there is no shared MUTABLE state across requests to protect, so a `Mutex` would add cost and complexity for no benefit. If a future feature needed live, mutable, shared state (e.g., an in-memory cache updated by concurrent requests), a `Mutex` (for occasional writes) or `RwLock` (for read-heavy access) would be the natural next tool — worth knowing even though the codebase hasn't needed it yet.

entries.title: RwLock<T> — many readers, or one writer
entries.l1: An `RwLock` ('read-write lock') is a more permissive `Mutex`: any number of readers can hold it at once, but a writer needs it all to itself with nobody else reading or writing. It's the right tool when reads vastly outnumber writes and you don't want every reader queuing behind every other reader. Not used anywhere in this codebase's Rust sources (checked across `server/` and `graph-types/`).
entries.l2:
`RwLock::new(value)`, then `.read()` for a shared guard or `.write()` for an exclusive one.

Example (illustrative, not from this repo):
```
use std::sync::RwLock;
let cache = RwLock::new(HashMap::new());
let snapshot = cache.read().unwrap(); // many of these can coexist
```
Newcomer mistake: assuming `RwLock` is strictly better than `Mutex` because it allows concurrent reads — it has more internal bookkeeping and can be slower under heavy write contention or short critical sections; choose based on the actual read/write ratio.
entries.l3: Absent from this codebase for the same structural reason as `Mutex`: the graph is loaded once and shared read-only via `Arc` (`server/atlas-cli/src/load.rs:22-23`), so there's no live read/write contention to arbitrate. If this project ever added a request-time mutable cache with many concurrent readers and occasional writers (e.g., memoizing an expensive computed view), `RwLock` would be the natural choice over `Mutex` specifically because reads there would vastly outnumber writes — worth knowing as the concept a newcomer will meet in the standard library even though this codebase hasn't needed it.

entries.title: OnceLock<T> — set once, read many times
entries.l1: `OnceLock<T>` is a box that starts empty and can be filled exactly once — after that, everyone who asks just gets the same already-computed value instead of redoing the work. It's the standard way to build something expensive (like loading a big test fixture) lazily the FIRST time it's needed, then reuse it for every subsequent call in the same process, which matters a lot for test suites that would otherwise reload gigabytes of data per test.
entries.l2:
`static CELL: OnceLock<T> = OnceLock::new();` then `CELL.get_or_init(|| expensive_computation())` — the closure runs at most once, no matter how many times or from how many threads `get_or_init` is called.

Example:
```
static CACHED: std::sync::OnceLock<atlas_core::data::AtlasData> = std::sync::OnceLock::new();
```
Newcomer mistake: reaching for a `lazy_static!`-style external crate macro out of old habit — `OnceLock` has been in `std` since Rust 1.70 and needs no extra dependency for this exact pattern.
entries.l3: `server/atlas-etl/tests/coverage.rs:438-441`, `server/atlas-graph/tests/artifact_conformance.rs:54`, and `server/atlas-graph/tests/attestation_exclusivity_real_data.rs:29,41` all use a `static CACHED: OnceLock<...>` (or `static GRAPH: OnceLock<atlas_graph_types::graph::Graph>`) to load the real committed data/graph exactly once per test binary, then share it across every test function in that file — the coverage.rs comment (line 438) notes it's a 'same-crate call, no layering question at all' and is cached specifically because reloading the real dataset per test would be slow. This is purely a test-performance pattern here, not a production runtime one.

entries.title: derive — generate boilerplate implementations
entries.l1: `#[derive(...)]` tells the compiler to write certain repetitive-but-mechanical code for you — 'give this type the ability to be compared for equality, printed for debugging, and cloned' — instead of you hand-writing near-identical code for every type. It's the difference between typing out 'how do I compare two of these' by hand fifty times and asking the compiler to do the mechanical part once, correctly, every time.
entries.l2:
`#[derive(Debug, Clone, PartialEq)]` above a `struct`/`enum` definition generates those traits' implementations automatically, based on the type's fields (all of which must also implement the trait being derived).

Example:
```
#[derive(Clone, Copy, Debug, PartialEq, Eq, PartialOrd, Ord, Hash)]
pub struct ContentHash(pub u64);
```
Newcomer mistake: deriving `Copy` on a type that owns a `String` or `Vec` — it won't compile, because `Copy` requires every field to also be trivially copyable (a heap-allocated `String` isn't); use `Clone` alone instead for those.
entries.l3: Derives are everywhere in this codebase: `server/atlas-core/src/data.rs:11,18,25,89,138` derives `Debug, Clone, Default, PartialEq, Serialize, Deserialize` on data-shape structs; `graph-types/src/id.rs:163` derives `Clone, Copy, Debug, PartialEq, Eq, PartialOrd, Ord, Hash` on `ContentHash` so it can be a `BTreeMap`/`BTreeSet` key AND compared cheaply by value. The `kind_tags!` macro (`graph-types/src/id.rs:38-39`) even derives the SAME trait set on fourteen generated zero-field tag structs in one stroke — derive plus a macro together eliminate what would otherwise be dozens of hand-written, error-prone `impl` blocks.

entries.title: macro_rules! — code that writes code
entries.l1: `macro_rules!` lets you define a pattern that expands into repetitive code at compile time — like a fill-in-the-blank template that generates several near-identical pieces of code from one compact table, instead of pasting the same shape by hand for every variant. `kind_tags!` takes a short list of 'name => kind' pairs and expands it into fourteen full struct-plus-trait-impl definitions.
entries.l3: `graph-types/src/id.rs:40-46` (`kind_tags!`) generates fourteen zero-sized tag structs plus their `KindTag` impls from one table (id.rs:48-61), each becoming the `K` in a `NodeId<K>` — see `phantom-type`. `graph-types/src/edge.rs:42` (`relations!`) similarly generates `RelationId`/`SymRelationId` enum variants plus their forward/inverse/symmetric `match` arms (edge.rs:25,56,59,66) from a compact table. `server/atlas-server/tests/contract_pact.rs:109` (`node_kind_manifest!`) and `server/atlas-graph/src/provenance.rs:112`/`tests/provenance_registry_real_data.rs:65` (`sweep!`) use local, function-scoped macros to avoid repeating a sweep pattern across many similar checks.

entries.title: attribute — a note to the compiler above an item
entries.l1: An attribute is a tag you put on a piece of code that tells the compiler (or a tool) to treat it specially — like a sticky note on a form saying 'process this one differently.' `#[derive(Debug)]` above a struct, `#[cfg(test)]` above a test module, `#[tokio::main]` above `fn main` — all attributes, all changing how that one item is compiled or generated, without changing the code's own logic.
entries.l2:
Written as `#[name]` or `#[name(args)]` directly above the item it applies to; `#![name]` (with a `!`) applies to the whole enclosing module or crate instead of the next item.

Example:
```
#[cfg(test)]
mod tests { ... }

#[tokio::main]
async fn main() -> anyhow::Result<()> { ... }
```
Newcomer mistake: confusing `#[attr]` (applies to the NEXT item) with `#![attr]` (applies to the ENCLOSING item, often the whole crate, usually seen at the very top of `lib.rs`/`main.rs`) — `graph-types/src/lib.rs:14` (`#![allow(dead_code)]`) is the crate-wide form.
entries.l3: This codebase uses attributes for: derives (`#[derive(...)]`, e.g. `graph-types/src/id.rs:163`), conditional compilation (`#[cfg(test)]`, `graph-types/src/graph.rs:514`), async entry points (`#[tokio::main]`, `server/atlas-server/src/main.rs:66`), test markers (`#[tokio::test]`, `server/atlas-server/src/contract.rs:42`), and crate-wide lint suppression (`#![allow(dead_code)]`, `graph-types/src/lib.rs:14` — an honest acknowledgment that a 'skeleton' crate has some currently-unused code). See `cfg`, `derive`, and `tokio` for the specific attribute families this codebase leans on most.

entries.title: visibility — what's public, what's private
entries.l1: Visibility controls who's allowed to see or use a piece of code — the difference between a public storefront and a back office. By default in Rust, everything is PRIVATE to its own module; you have to explicitly mark something `pub` for code outside that module to reach it. This is a deliberate safety net: internal helpers can be refactored freely because the compiler can prove nothing outside the module depends on them.
entries.l2:
`pub` makes an item visible everywhere the crate is reachable from (and re-exportable outside it); `pub(crate)` makes it visible anywhere in the SAME crate but nowhere outside; no modifier means visible only within the current module and its children.

Example:
```
pub(crate) fn year_index(y: Year) -> i64 { ... }
```
Newcomer mistake: marking everything `pub` 'just in case' — that turns every internal detail into part of your public API, which then can't change later without breaking callers. Default to private, and widen only what genuinely needs to be reached from outside.
entries.l3: `graph-types/src/lib.rs:35-40`'s `pub mod covenant` is the DELIBERATE, narrow public surface a sibling map-system project is allowed to depend on — everything else in the crate can change freely. `server/atlas-core/src/data.rs:2019` (`pub(crate) fn year_index`) and `server/atlas-cli/src/commands/find.rs:30-31` (`pub(crate) const SEARCHED_KINDS`/`EXCLUDED_KINDS`) use crate-internal visibility for helpers shared across a crate's own modules but never meant for outside callers. This distinction (`pub` vs `pub(crate)` vs private) is how the 'covenant' promise in `lib.rs` is actually enforced by the compiler, not just documentation.

entries.title: newtype — wrapping one type to give it a new identity
entries.l1: A newtype is a struct with exactly one field, used purely to give a plain value (a number, a string) its OWN distinct type — like putting a plain dollar bill in a labeled envelope so it can't be mistaken for a euro bill even though both are just paper. `ContentHash(u64)` is 'a u64, but specifically a content hash' — you can't accidentally pass a page count where a content hash was expected, because they're different types even though both are secretly a `u64`.
entries.l3: `graph-types/src/id.rs:164` (`pub struct ContentHash(pub u64);`) prevents a raw hash number from being confused with any other `u64` in the codebase. Error types follow the same pattern throughout `atlas-graph`: `ArtifactError(pub String)` (`server/atlas-graph/src/artifact.rs:64`), `FidelityViolation(pub String)` (`fidelity.rs:63`), `FulfillmentGroundingViolation(pub String)` (`fulfillment_adapter.rs:114`), `PeoplesFidelityViolation`/`NamedAfterGroundingViolation` (`peoples_adapter.rs:307,414`), `PersonFidelityViolation` (`person_adapter.rs:169`) — each a one-field wrapper around a message, each with its own `Display` impl, so a `match`/`?` chain can never confuse one violation kind for another even though they're all 'just a String' underneath.

entries.title: phantom-type — a type parameter with no runtime data
entries.l1: A phantom type is a type parameter that exists ONLY at compile time to keep the compiler honest — it adds zero bytes to the value at runtime, but lets the compiler tell apart things that would otherwise look identical. `NodeId<PlaceTag>` and `NodeId<PersonTag>` are both, underneath, just a stored string — but the compiler will never let you accidentally compare a Place id to a Person id, because they're different TYPES even though they're the same SHAPE.
entries.l3: `graph-types/src/id.rs:67` (`pub struct NodeId<K: KindTag>(pub Interned, pub PhantomData<K>);`) is this codebase's central phantom-typed identity: the doc comment above `KindTag` (id.rs:32-33) states the payoff directly — 'a cross-kind reference is a type error, not a runtime surprise.' At runtime, every `NodeId<K>` is exactly as large as the `Interned` string it wraps; the `K` and its `PhantomData<K>` marker vanish entirely after compilation (monomorphization — see `generics`), so this safety costs nothing in memory or speed.

entries.title: type-alias — a nickname for a type
entries.l1: A type alias gives an existing type a new, more meaningful name — the type itself doesn't change, only what you call it. `type Interned = String;` doesn't create a new kind of thing; it just lets the rest of the codebase say 'an Interned' instead of 'a String' in places where that name communicates INTENT (this string is meant to be a deduplicated, interned identifier) even though, today, it's really nothing more than a plain `String`.
entries.l2:
`type Name = ExistingType;` — usable anywhere `ExistingType` is, interchangeably; the compiler does NOT distinguish `Interned` from `String` the way it would a newtype (see `newtype`) wrapping the same thing.

Example:
```
pub type Interned = String;
pub type EdgeSummary = BTreeMap<EdgeKind, usize>;
```
Newcomer mistake: reaching for a type alias when you actually want type-level SAFETY (preventing mix-ups) — an alias is purely a readability nickname; two aliases for the same underlying type are still fully interchangeable to the compiler, unlike two different newtypes.
entries.l3: `graph-types/src/id.rs:8` (`pub type Interned = String;`) is explicitly called a 'skeleton stand-in for a future interner' by the comment right above it, and the crate's own top-level doc comment (`lib.rs:11`) discloses it as a deliberate simplification — a real interning pool is anticipated but not built (see `interning`). `graph-types/src/explore.rs:46` (`pub type EdgeSummary = BTreeMap<EdgeKind, usize>`) and `graph-types/src/ingest.rs:14` (`pub type ProvenanceId = Interned;`) use aliases purely for readability at call sites, so a function signature reads 'returns an EdgeSummary' rather than a bare, unexplained `BTreeMap<EdgeKind, usize>`.

entries.title: const & static — values baked in at compile time
entries.l1: `const` and `static` both declare a value that's fixed before the program even starts running — the difference from a regular variable is that these exist for the WHOLE program's lifetime and never move. `const` is more like a name for a literal value, copy-pasted wherever it's used; `static` is one single, fixed memory location shared by everyone who reads it — which is why `static` is what you reach for when you need something built once and then reused (like a cached test fixture).
entries.l3: `graph-types/src/id.rs:35` (`const KIND: NodeKind;` on the `KindTag` trait) and its fourteen implementations generated by `kind_tags!` (id.rs:41) are associated constants — each tag struct's `KindTag::KIND` is resolved entirely at compile time. `server/atlas-etl/tests/coverage.rs:441` (`static CACHED: OnceLock<AtlasData> = OnceLock::new();`) is the `static` form, paired with `OnceLock` for safe one-time lazy initialization rather than eager static data. `server/atlas-cli/src/commands/find.rs:30-31` uses `pub(crate) const` for two fixed lookup strings.

entries.title: Default — a sensible empty/starting value
entries.l1: The `Default` trait gives a type a standard 'starting' or 'empty' value you can ask for without spelling out every field — like a form that comes pre-filled with reasonable blanks instead of you typing zero into every box by hand. `Graph::default()` gives you an empty graph — no nodes, no edges yet — ready to be filled in during the build step.
entries.l3: `graph-types/src/graph.rs:24-25` (`#[derive(Debug, Default)] pub struct Graph`) and `ReadingSpine` (graph.rs:20-21) both derive `Default`, giving the build pipeline (`server/atlas-graph/src/pipeline.rs`) a clean, empty starting graph to progressively fill as each pass runs. `server/atlas-core/src/data.rs:11,18` derives `Default` alongside `Serialize`/`Deserialize` on several data-shape structs, useful both for tests constructing partial fixtures and for JSON deserialization filling in optional/missing fields.

entries.title: Clone & Copy — duplicating a value
entries.l1: `Clone` and `Copy` both mean 'you can duplicate this value', but for different costs and different kinds of data. `Copy` is for small, simple values (numbers, and structs made purely of them) — duplicating them is so cheap it happens automatically, silently, every time you'd otherwise 'move' them (see `ownership`). `Clone` is for anything that might be expensive to duplicate (a `String`, a `Vec`, anything with heap data) — you have to explicitly call `.clone()`, so the cost is always visible in the code, never hidden.
entries.l2:
`#[derive(Clone)]` adds a `.clone()` method (deep-copies); `#[derive(Copy)]` (requires `Clone` too) makes the type implicitly duplicate on every use instead of moving — only legal if every field is itself `Copy` (no `String`, `Vec`, `Box`, etc.).

Example:
```
#[derive(Clone, Copy, Debug, PartialEq, Eq, PartialOrd, Ord, Hash)]
pub struct ContentHash(pub u64);
```
Newcomer mistake: sprinkling `.clone()` everywhere to silence a borrow-checker complaint without understanding why it was complaining — it usually compiles, but can paper over a design that should be borrowing instead of duplicating; see `borrowing`.
entries.l3: `graph-types/src/id.rs:163` derives `Copy` on `ContentHash` (a plain `u64` wrapper — free to duplicate) but the fourteen `kind_tags!`-generated tag structs (`id.rs:38-39`) ALSO derive `Copy` since they're zero-sized markers with nothing to actually copy. `NodeId<K>` itself (id.rs:66, `#[derive(Debug)]` only) is deliberately NOT `Copy` (it owns a `String`) — cloning it explicitly (`.clone()`, id.rs:81) is a visible, intentional operation, matching the general rule: identity-carrying, potentially-expensive values stay `Clone`-only; small value-like markers are `Copy`.

entries.title: Debug & Display — two ways to print a value
entries.l1: Rust splits 'turn this into text' into two separate traits with two separate purposes. `Debug` (`{:?}`) is the programmer's view — dump everything, field names included, for debugging; you almost always just derive it. `Display` (`{}`) is the human-facing view — a message a USER should read, like an error message — and you write it by hand because only you know what a good user-facing message looks like.
entries.l3: `Debug` is derived nearly everywhere in this codebase (e.g. `graph-types/src/graph.rs:24`, `server/atlas-core/src/data.rs:11`). `Display` is hand-implemented specifically on error types, since THOSE messages are meant to be read by a human running the CLI or hitting an HTTP endpoint: `server/atlas-graph/src/artifact.rs:65` (`ArtifactError`), `server/atlas-cli/src/error.rs:102` (`CliError`), `server/atlas-core/src/refs.rs:104` (`ScriptureRef`), `fidelity.rs:65`, `fulfillment_adapter.rs:116` (`FulfillmentGroundingViolation`) — each turns its wrapped `String` (see `newtype`) into a clean, user-facing message rather than a debug dump of internal fields.

entries.title: From & Into — type conversions the compiler can chain
entries.l1: `From`/`Into` are how Rust standardizes 'convert this type into that type' so the conversion can be used generically, not just called by a specific method name. If `TypeB` implements `From<TypeA>`, you automatically get `TypeA`'s `.into()` to produce a `TypeB` too — implement one direction, get both usable forms for free. This is also the machinery behind `impl Into<Interned>` as a function parameter: 'accept anything that can become an Interned', so callers can pass a `String`, a `&str`, or anything else that converts.
entries.l3: `graph-types/src/id.rs:70` (`pub fn new(raw: impl Into<Interned>) -> Self`) accepts anything convertible into the `Interned` (`String`) type, then calls `.into()` (id.rs:71) to perform the conversion exactly once — this is a trait-bound in argument position (see `trait-bound`) built directly on `Into`. `?`-propagated errors (see `?-operator`) also rely on `From`: a `thiserror` `#[source]` field (`server/atlas-core/src/lib.rs:29,31`) works with `?` precisely because `thiserror` generates a `From` conversion from the source error into `CoreError`.

entries.title: Ord & PartialOrd — putting values in order
entries.l1: `PartialOrd`/`Ord` let the compiler compare two values and say which comes first — like giving playing cards a rank so they can be sorted into a deck. `PartialOrd` allows for pairs that CAN'T be compared (like NaN with floating-point numbers); `Ord` promises every pair CAN always be ordered, which is required for anything used as a `BTreeMap`/`BTreeSet` key, since those containers need to always know where a new item belongs.
entries.l2:
`#[derive(PartialOrd, Ord)]` generates a field-by-field, top-to-bottom comparison (like comparing tuples lexicographically). Required for `BTreeMap`/`BTreeSet` keys and for `.sort()`.

Example:
```
#[derive(Clone, Debug, PartialEq, Eq, PartialOrd, Ord, Hash)]
pub struct Pid {
    pub kind: PositionKind,
    pub hash: ContentHash,
}
```
Newcomer mistake: deriving `Ord` and expecting a MEANINGFUL sort order without checking field declaration order — the derived comparison goes field-by-field in the order they're WRITTEN in the struct, so `Pid`'s ordering is 'by kind first, then by hash', not the other way around, purely because `kind` is declared first.
entries.l3: `graph-types/src/id.rs:163,166` derive `Ord`/`PartialOrd` on `ContentHash` and `Pid` so they can be `BTreeMap`/`BTreeSet` keys and produce a deterministic sort — see `sort-determinism`. `AnyNodeId` (used as the key of `Graph::nodes: BTreeMap<AnyNodeId, Node>`, `graph-types/src/graph.rs:27`) needs the same derives for the same reason: the artifact dump's byte-determinism (`server/atlas-graph/tests/determinism.rs`) depends on every BTree-keyed type having a total, derived order.

entries.title: Hash — turning a value into a lookup key
entries.l1: The `Hash` trait lets a value be turned into a number suitable for fast lookup — it's what makes a type usable as a `HashMap` key. Two equal values must always hash to the same number (otherwise the lookup table would lose track of them), which is why `Hash` is almost always derived TOGETHER with `Eq`, never on its own.
entries.l3: `graph-types/src/id.rs:101` and `graph-types/src/text.rs:140,191` hand-write `fn hash<H: Hasher>(&self, st: &mut H)` rather than deriving it — a deliberate choice for types where the derived (all-fields) hash wouldn't match the type's own custom `PartialEq`. `ContentHash`/`Pid` (id.rs:163,166) derive `Hash` normally, since content-addressed identity needs no custom logic: the whole point of a `ContentHash` is that its bytes ARE the identity, so the default field-based hash is exactly right — see `content-hash`.

entries.title: error-handling — failures as named, typed values
entries.l1: Rust treats 'something went wrong' as an ordinary value passed back through a return type, not a surprise thrown across your program. Instead of catching an unpredictable exception that could come from anywhere, a function's signature TELLS you it might fail (`Result`), and what kinds of failure to expect (an error enum listing them). It reads almost like a form with checkboxes for every way a task can go wrong, rather than a blank 'something broke' message.
entries.l2:
The idiom: define an error enum with one variant per real failure mode (often via `#[derive(Debug, thiserror::Error)]` — see `thiserror`), have fallible functions return `Result<T, YourError>`, and propagate with `?` (see `?-operator`).

Example:
```
#[derive(Debug, Error)]
pub enum CoreError {
    #[error("io error reading {path}")]
    Io { path: String, #[source] source: std::io::Error },
    #[error("json error reading {path}")]
    Json { path: String, #[source] source: serde_json::Error },
}
```
Newcomer mistake: reaching for `panic!`/`.unwrap()` for anything a CALLER might reasonably want to recover from — reserve panics for truly unrecoverable bugs (see `panic-unwrap-expect`), and model expected failures as `Result` instead.
entries.l3: `server/atlas-core/src/lib.rs:20-31` (`CoreError`) is the library-level pattern: a closed, matchable set of failure modes. `server/atlas-graph/src/artifact.rs:64-65`, `fidelity.rs:63-65`, `fulfillment_adapter.rs:114-116`, `peoples_adapter.rs:307,414`, `person_adapter.rs:169` each define a small newtype error (see `newtype`) with its own `Display` message instead of sharing one generic error type — a deliberate choice so a `match`/`?` chain can distinguish e.g. a fidelity violation from a grounding violation. ETL binaries use `anyhow` instead (see `anyhow`) at the top level, where propagate-and-report is all that's needed.

entries.title: anyhow — one flexible error type for application code
entries.l1: `anyhow` is a small crate that gives you one universal 'something went wrong, here's a message and maybe a cause chain' error type, so you don't have to design a custom error enum for every binary or script. It's meant for the TOP of a program — a CLI tool or ETL script — where you mostly want to report a clear failure and exit, not carefully match on which of ten specific things happened.
entries.l3: `server/atlas-etl/src/bins/gen_sources.rs:29`, `brainfuel.rs:111`, `catechism_map.rs:43`, `compile.rs:37`, `concord.rs:78` all `use anyhow::{Context, Result}` (some with `bail`) for ETL parsing and compilation, where the ETL binary's job is 'transform source files or fail with a clear message', not offer a matchable API. `server/atlas-server/src/bins/export_aqc_examples.rs:53-54` (`#[tokio::main] async fn main() -> anyhow::Result<()>`) is the same pattern at a binary's entry point. This is the deliberate split this codebase draws: `anyhow` in binaries/ETL scripts, `thiserror` enums in libraries.

entries.title: thiserror — deriving proper error enums
entries.l1: `thiserror` is a small crate that removes the tedious, error-prone boilerplate of hand-writing `Display` and `std::error::Error` for a custom error enum. You write the enum and a `#[error("...")]` message template per variant; `thiserror` derives the rest. It's the difference between hand-writing a formatting function for every failure case and just annotating each case with the message it should show.
entries.l2:
`#[derive(Debug, thiserror::Error)]` on an enum; each variant gets `#[error("message with {field} interpolation")]`; a field can be tagged `#[source]` to wire it into the standard `Error::source()` chain (which is what lets tools print 'caused by: ...' chains, and what lets `?` convert an underlying error automatically).

Example:
```
#[derive(Debug, Error)]
pub enum CoreError {
    #[error("io error reading {path}")]
    Io { path: String, #[source] source: std::io::Error },
}
```
Newcomer mistake: forgetting `#[source]` on the wrapped underlying error — without it, `?` won't automatically convert that error type into yours, and error-chain tools won't show the original cause.
entries.l3: `server/atlas-core/src/lib.rs:18,20-31` is this codebase's one `thiserror` use: `use thiserror::Error;` then `#[derive(Debug, Error)] pub enum CoreError { Io { path: String, #[source] source: std::io::Error }, Json { path: String, #[source] source: serde_json::Error }, ... }`. This is the library-facing counterpart to `anyhow`'s binary-facing convenience (see `anyhow`) — `atlas-core` callers can `match` on exactly which of `CoreError`'s variants occurred, something an `anyhow::Error` deliberately doesn't support.

entries.title: panic! / unwrap / expect — giving up on purpose
entries.l1: `panic!`, `.unwrap()`, and `.expect()` are Rust's way of saying 'this should be IMPOSSIBLE, and if it happens anyway, stop everything rather than continue with corrupted assumptions.' Unlike a `Result`-based error, a panic isn't meant to be recovered from by ordinary code — it's a program-crashing assertion that a bug exists. Using them means: 'I've decided this failure means the program is broken, not that the caller made a normal mistake.'
entries.l2:
`panic!("message")` stops the current thread immediately. `.unwrap()` on an `Option`/`Result` panics if it's `None`/`Err`; `.expect("message")` does the same but with a custom panic message explaining WHY you believed it couldn't fail.

Example:
```
Command::new(env!("CARGO_BIN_EXE_bibex")).args(args).output().expect("bibex must run")
```
Newcomer mistake: reaching for `.unwrap()` in ordinary application logic 'to get it compiling', then shipping it — a `None`/`Err` there becomes a hard crash for a real user. `.unwrap()`/`.expect()` are fine in tests (where a failure SHOULD stop the test loudly) and genuinely-impossible cases; anywhere else, propagate the error instead (see `?-operator`).
entries.l3: `server/atlas-cli/tests/cli.rs:17` (`.output().expect("bibex must run")`) and `server/atlas-cli/tests/contract_pact_cli.rs:93` use `.expect()` in TEST code, where a failure to even run the binary under test should abort the test suite loudly and immediately — an appropriate, deliberate use. Production request-handling code in `server/atlas-server/src/graph_handlers.rs` instead returns `Result<Json<...>, ApiError>` (e.g. `graph_handlers.rs:123`) rather than unwrapping, converting a missing node into a proper HTTP error response instead of crashing the server process for one bad request.

entries.title: doc-comment — documentation the compiler checks
entries.l1: A doc comment (`///` above an item, or `//!` at the top of a file/module) is documentation that tools actually understand — it can be turned into a browsable reference (`cargo doc`), and any code examples inside it can be run as tests (`cargo test` executes doc examples too), so stale documentation that no longer matches the code tends to get caught automatically. This codebase's doc comments are unusually long and narrative — they explain WHY a design decision was made, not just WHAT a function does.
entries.l3: `graph-types/src/lib.rs:1-12` (crate-level `//!`) and `graph-types/src/id.rs:1,9-12,32-33` (module- and item-level docs) are representative: long, narrative comments explaining the DESIGN rationale ('a cross-kind reference is a type error, not a runtime surprise') alongside disclosed simplifications ('Interned is a String; the content hash is a 64-bit std hash'). The brief for this very glossary notes these doc comments cite past work batches by name (e.g. 'M-C', 'PROV-1') — treat those as historical context markers, not something to explain to a reader.

entries.title: cfg — compile this only under some condition
entries.l1: `#[cfg(...)]` tells the compiler 'only include this code when a certain condition holds' — most commonly, 'only when running tests.' It's how test-only helper code and production code can live in the SAME file without the test code ever being compiled into the real, shipped binary — no separate test project needed, no risk of test helpers accidentally leaking into production.
entries.l3: `graph-types/src/graph.rs:514-515` (`#[cfg(test)] mod tests { use super::*; ... }`) and `graph-types/src/frontier.rs:589` are examples of this codebase's standard pattern: unit tests live at the bottom of the same file as the code they test, gated so they never ship. Integration tests (see `integration-test`) don't need `#[cfg(test)]` at all — files under a crate's `tests/` directory are automatically test-only by their location, not by an attribute.

entries.title: feature-flag — a switch compiled into (or out of) the build
entries.l1: A feature flag is an on/off switch decided before the program runs — either 'compile this optional piece of code in or out' (Cargo's own feature mechanism) or, more loosely, 'this behavior is currently on, and could be flipped off in one place.' This Rust codebase's `Cargo.toml` files don't define any Cargo `[features]` sections, so the closest real example of the CONCEPT lives on the client side instead.
entries.l3: No `[features]` section exists in any `Cargo.toml` under `server/` (checked directly) — this codebase's Rust crates don't use Cargo's conditional-compilation feature mechanism at all. The real analog is `client/FeatureFlags.cs:1-28`, a `static readonly bool XrefSuperscripts` gate whose own doc comment explains a `static readonly` (not `const`) was chosen deliberately: a `const false` made a render branch provably unreachable and tripped a compiler warning (CS0162) on an otherwise warning-free build. It's a runtime-checked, compile-time-set switch — one home for flags, not scattered magic booleans.

entries.title: unsafe — code the compiler can't fully check for you
entries.l1: `unsafe` is an escape hatch: a small, explicitly marked region where YOU take over responsibility for guarantees the compiler normally enforces automatically (like never reading freed memory). This codebase deliberately doesn't use it — the whole point of choosing safe alternatives (like `thread::scope` instead of raw threads with shared pointers) is to get the SAME capability without ever needing to open that escape hatch.
entries.l2:
`unsafe { ... }` blocks (or `unsafe fn`) are required for a handful of specific operations: dereferencing raw pointers, calling other `unsafe` functions, mutating a `static`, and a few others. Nothing about `unsafe` disables the borrow checker everywhere — it only unlocks those specific operations, and everything else in the block is still checked normally.

Example: none needed here — this codebase's own comment on its hardest concurrency problem states outright that its solution is 'safe, unsafe-free data parallelism.'
