Newcomer mistake: assuming `unsafe` means 'anything goes' — it doesn't disable Rust's type system or most of its checks; it only permits a specific, narrow set of extra operations, and misusing THOSE can still cause real memory bugs.
entries.l3: A search across every `.rs` file in `server/` and `graph-types/` found no `unsafe` keyword usage at all. `graph-types/src/graph.rs:111` explicitly calls out the alternative this codebase chose for its one genuinely tricky concurrency problem (building the artifact in parallel across `std::thread::available_parallelism()` worker threads): 'That's safe, unsafe-free data parallelism' via `std::thread::scope` (see `scoped-threads`), where the borrow checker itself proves no two threads can touch the same data — the guarantee `unsafe` code would otherwise have to hand-verify.

entries.title: threads — running code at the same time
entries.l1: A thread is a separate line of execution running alongside your main program — like having several workers on the same job at once instead of one worker doing everything in sequence. This codebase uses threads specifically to speed up building the graph artifact: split the work into chunks, hand each chunk to its own thread, and combine the results once they're all done.
entries.l2:
`std::thread::available_parallelism()` asks the OS how many CPU cores are usable; the actual spawning here uses SCOPED threads (see `scoped-threads`) rather than the more familiar `std::thread::spawn`, which this codebase doesn't use anywhere.

Example:
```
let n_threads = std::thread::available_parallelism()
    .map(|n| n.get())
    .unwrap_or(4);
```
Newcomer mistake: assuming more threads always means faster — beyond the number of CPU cores, extra threads just add scheduling overhead without more real parallelism; `available_parallelism()` is exactly how this codebase avoids over-subscribing the machine.
entries.l3: `server/atlas-graph/src/artifact.rs:1388-1417` computes `n_threads` from `std::thread::available_parallelism()` and uses it to size chunks for the parallel build step (artifact.rs:1417,1430) — a comment right above (artifact.rs:1388-1389) frames this as a deliberate 'tier' choice. No use of plain `std::thread::spawn` (the un-scoped, detached form) appears anywhere in this codebase; every threaded computation here goes through `std::thread::scope` instead — see `scoped-threads` for why that's the safer, chosen alternative.

entries.title: std::thread::scope — threads that can't outlive their data
entries.l1: A scoped thread is a worker thread that the program GUARANTEES will finish before moving on — which means it's allowed to borrow data from outside instead of needing its own full copy. Regular threads can outlive the function that spawned them, so they can only safely borrow data that lives forever (or that they own outright); a `thread::scope` block promises 'everything spawned inside here finishes before we leave this block', so borrowing short-lived data across threads becomes safe and compiler-checked.
entries.l3: `server/atlas-graph/src/artifact.rs:1430` (`std::thread::scope(|scope| -> Result<_, ArtifactError> { ... })`) splits node-processing work into chunks across `available_parallelism()` threads (see `threads`), each chunk closure built with `.map(|chunk| scope.spawn(move || ...))` (`graph-types/src/graph.rs:408`). `graph-types/src/graph.rs:111-112,393` explicitly frames this as the reason the parallel build needs no `unsafe` code and no shared mutable state crossing a thread boundary — each spawned closure owns (via `move`) its own chunk, and results are collected only once every thread has rejoined at the end of the `scope`.

entries.title: channels — passing messages between threads
entries.l1: A channel is a pipe for sending values from one thread to another safely — one end sends, the other receives, and the runtime handles the handoff without either side touching the other's memory directly. This codebase's own search turned up no channel usage anywhere in its Rust sources; its one multi-threaded workload (building the graph artifact) doesn't need one.
entries.l3: No `mpsc::channel` or similar message-passing primitive appears anywhere in `server/` or `graph-types/`. The parallel artifact build (`server/atlas-graph/src/artifact.rs:1430`, `graph-types/src/graph.rs:408`) gets results back from each `scope.spawn`'d closure simply by RETURNING a value from the closure and collecting the `JoinHandle`s' results directly — no message passing needed, since each thread does one bounded chunk of work and then the whole `thread::scope` block ends. Channels would matter more for an ongoing producer/consumer pattern, which this codebase doesn't currently have.

entries.title: async / await — pausable functions
entries.l1: `async`/`await` let a function pause while it's waiting on something slow (like a network response) WITHOUT blocking the whole program — the runtime can go do other work during that wait, then come back and resume exactly where it left off. Every HTTP request handler in the web server is written this way: it can 'wait' for the graph to answer a query without freezing every OTHER request being handled at the same time.
entries.l3: Every axum handler in `server/atlas-server/src/graph_handlers.rs` (e.g. `node_card` at line 123, `node_edges` at 198, `text_window` at 348) and `server/atlas-server/src/handlers.rs:29` (`pub async fn health()`) is `async`, matching axum's requirement that route handlers be async functions the runtime can juggle across many simultaneous requests. `server/atlas-server/src/contract.rs:34,42` shows both an async handler and an `#[tokio::test] async fn` test calling it directly.

entries.title: tokio — the engine that runs async code
entries.l1: `async`/`await` alone doesn't run anything — you need a RUNTIME that actually schedules and drives all those pausable functions, juggling them across however many worker threads make sense. `tokio` is that runtime: the thing that lets the web server handle many requests 'at once' by switching between them whenever one is waiting rather than truly running them all in true parallel on separate CPU cores exclusively.
entries.l3: `server/atlas-server/src/main.rs:66` (`#[tokio::main]`) boots the whole web server's async runtime. `server/atlas-server/src/contract.rs:42` and `server/atlas-server/tests/api.rs:121,140` use `#[tokio::test]` to run individual async test functions each on their own tiny tokio runtime, without needing a full server process. `server/atlas-server/src/bins/export_aqc_examples.rs:53-54` shows the same `#[tokio::main]` pattern powering a smaller utility binary that captures API examples rather than the main server.

entries.title: axum — the web framework serving the API
entries.l1: `axum` is the toolkit that turns 'a function that answers a query' into 'an HTTP endpoint the Blazor client can call.' It maps URLs (like `/api/node/:id`) to handler functions, handles the plumbing of requests and responses, and lets you plug in shared state (like the loaded graph) that every handler can reach. It's the same role Express, Flask, or ASP.NET Core plays in other stacks.
entries.l2:
`axum::Router::new().route("/path", get(handler_fn))` builds up the URL-to-handler map; `State(shared_value)` as a handler parameter gives that handler access to state registered once at startup (e.g. the loaded graph, wrapped in `Arc` — see `Arc`).

Example:
```
let api = Router::new()
    .route("/api/node/:id", get(node_card));
```
Newcomer mistake: expecting handler functions to share MUTABLE state casually — axum encourages read-mostly shared state via `State<Arc<T>>`; genuine shared mutation needs its own synchronization (a `Mutex`/`RwLock`), which this codebase currently avoids entirely by keeping the graph immutable after load.
entries.l3: `server/atlas-server/src/app.rs:11,132` (`use axum::Router; let api = Router::new()...`) builds this server's route table; `server/atlas-server/src/graph_handlers.rs:123,198,348` (`node_card`, `node_edges`, `text_window`) are handler functions taking `State(graph): State<Arc<GraphService>>` to reach the shared, loaded graph. `server/atlas-server/tests/api.rs:100` (`fn app() -> axum::Router`) builds the same router for integration tests, so tests exercise the real routing/handler wiring rather than calling handler functions directly in isolation.

entries.title: serde — converting Rust values to and from data formats
entries.l1: `serde` is the standard way Rust code turns its own values into JSON (or other formats) and back — the bridge between 'a struct in memory' and 'text a web client or a saved file can understand.' Rather than hand-writing 'read this field, then that field' parsing code for every struct, you tag the struct once and `serde` generates the conversion.
entries.l2:
`#[derive(Serialize, Deserialize)]` on a struct/enum generates the conversion code; combined with `serde_json` it becomes `serde_json::to_string(&value)` / `serde_json::from_str(&text)`.

Example:
```
#[derive(Debug, Clone, Default, PartialEq, Serialize, Deserialize)]
pub struct SomeDto { pub field: String }
```
Newcomer mistake: assuming field NAMES automatically match a different naming convention on the wire (like `snake_case` Rust fields vs. `camelCase` JSON) — serde needs an explicit `#[serde(rename = "...")]` or a container-level rename rule for that; it won't guess.
entries.l3: `server/atlas-core/src/data.rs:11,18,25,89,138` derives `Serialize, Deserialize` (alongside `Debug, Clone, Default, PartialEq`) on the data-shape structs the ETL pipeline reads from JSON source files and the server later re-serializes for API responses. `server/atlas-server/src/contract.rs` and `graph_handlers.rs` use `Json<T>` (axum's serde-backed response wrapper) to turn handler return values directly into JSON HTTP responses — see `axum`.

entries.title: bincode — a compact binary format for Rust values
entries.l1: `bincode` turns a Rust value directly into a tight binary byte sequence (and back) — no field names, no human-readable text, just the raw data laid out efficiently. It's the format the project's compiled graph artifact is stored in: smaller and faster to load than JSON would be, at the cost of not being human-readable if you open the file directly.
entries.l2:
`bincode::serialize(&value) -> Result<Vec<u8>, _>` and `bincode::deserialize(&bytes) -> Result<T, _>` — the type being (de)serialized needs `serde`'s `Serialize`/`Deserialize` derives (see `serde`), since `bincode` is a serde-compatible format, not its own separate derive.

Example:
```
bincode::serialize(d).map_err(|e| ArtifactError(format!("bincode encode failed: {e}")))
```
Newcomer mistake: expecting a `bincode`-encoded file to be readable in a text editor or diffable in a normal way like JSON — it's a dense binary format; verifying its contents means decoding it back into Rust values (or comparing raw bytes, as this codebase's own determinism test does) rather than reading it directly.
entries.l3: `server/atlas-graph/src/artifact.rs:1755,1759` (`bincode::serialize(d)...`, `bincode::deserialize(bytes)...`) encodes and decodes the compiled `data/compiled/graph.bin` artifact — the single file the whole server loads at startup. `server/atlas-graph/tests/determinism.rs` builds this artifact TWICE from the same real sources and asserts the encoded BYTES are byte-for-byte identical, a stronger check than comparing decoded values, since it also catches accidental non-determinism in field ORDER — see `sort-determinism`.

entries.title: std::process::Command — running another program
entries.l1: `std::process::Command` lets Rust code launch ANOTHER program as a subprocess and capture what it prints — like a script calling out to a separate tool and reading its output. This codebase's CLI tests use it to run the REAL, compiled `bibex` command-line binary (not a stand-in or mock) and check its actual printed output, which is a stronger test than calling internal functions directly.
entries.l2:
`Command::new("program").args(["arg1", "arg2"]).output()` runs the program and returns its captured stdout/stderr/exit code (wrapped in `Result`/`io::Result`).

Example:
```
Command::new(env!("CARGO_BIN_EXE_bibex")).args(args).output().expect("bibex must run")
```
Newcomer mistake: assuming a test that calls a crate's functions DIRECTLY is equivalent to testing the actual compiled binary — argument parsing, exit codes, and printed output are only genuinely exercised by running the real executable via `Command`, which is exactly what `env!("CARGO_BIN_EXE_bibex")` (see `env-macro`) gives you: the path to the test's own freshly-built binary.
entries.l3: `server/atlas-cli/tests/cli.rs:2,17` and `server/atlas-cli/tests/contract_pact_cli.rs:33,93` both run the real `bibex` binary via `Command::new(env!("CARGO_BIN_EXE_bibex"))`, treating the CLI's actual observable behavior (its printed text, its exit status) as the thing under test — the `cli.rs` header comment (line 2) says this directly: tests run `std::process::Command`, against the REAL committed binary, not an in-process shortcut. `graph-types/tests/toolchain_pin.rs:11` uses the same tool to shell out to `cargo`/`rustc` and check the pinned toolchain version.

entries.title: PathBuf — an owned, cross-platform file path
entries.l1: `PathBuf` is Rust's owned representation of a file-system path — built to work correctly whether the program runs on Windows (`\`) or Linux/Mac (`/`) without you hand-splicing separator characters. It's what you build up and pass around when you need to OWN a path (versus `&Path`, a borrowed view of one, the same owned/borrowed split as `String`/`&str`).
entries.l2:
`PathBuf::from("some/path")` creates one; `.join("more")` appends a segment (handling the separator correctly for the current OS); `Path::new("x")` gives a borrowed `&Path` when you don't need ownership.

Example:
```
pub fn default_data_dir() -> PathBuf {
    PathBuf::from("../data/compiled")
}
```
Newcomer mistake: building paths with string concatenation (`format!("{}/{}", dir, file)`) instead of `.join()` — that hardcodes the wrong separator on the other OS and mishandles edge cases `.join()` gets right automatically.
entries.l3: `server/atlas-cli/src/load.rs:13,63-64` (`use std::path::{Path, PathBuf}; pub fn default_data_dir() -> PathBuf { PathBuf::from("../data/compiled") }`) is where the CLI decides where to look for the compiled graph artifact by default. `server/atlas-cli/src/main.rs:13,55` uses `PathBuf` for parsing a `--data-dir`-style argument out of the command line (`extract_data_dir`). Tests build paths relative to the crate manifest with `Path::new(env!("CARGO_MANIFEST_DIR")).join(...)` (`server/atlas-cli/tests/cli.rs:13`) rather than assuming a fixed working directory.

entries.title: env!() — reading build-time environment into your code
entries.l1: `env!("VAR")` reads an environment variable AT COMPILE TIME and bakes its value directly into the compiled program as a string — different from `std::env::var("VAR")`, which reads it fresh every time the program RUNS. Cargo sets several useful variables automatically during a build, like the crate's own source directory or the path to a just-built sibling binary, which is exactly what this codebase's tests rely on.
entries.l2:
`env!("CARGO_MANIFEST_DIR")` expands (at compile time) to the absolute path of the crate's own directory; `env!("CARGO_BIN_EXE_name")` expands to the path of a just-built binary target named `name`, available only inside that crate's own tests.

Example:
```
Path::new(env!("CARGO_MANIFEST_DIR")).join("../../data/compiled")
```
Newcomer mistake: confusing `env!(...)` (a compile-time macro, fails to COMPILE if the variable is unset) with `std::env::var(...)` (a runtime function call, returns a `Result` you check at runtime) — they look similar but resolve at completely different times.
entries.l3: `server/atlas-cli/tests/cli.rs:4,13,17` and `server/atlas-cli/tests/contract_pact_cli.rs:11,38` use `env!("CARGO_MANIFEST_DIR")` to locate test fixtures relative to the crate root regardless of the current working directory, and `env!("CARGO_BIN_EXE_bibex")` to get the exact path Cargo just built the `bibex` binary to — the `contract_pact_cli.rs:11` comment notes this variable 'is defined only for the tests of' the crate that actually builds that binary target, a Cargo-specific gotcha worth knowing before reusing this pattern elsewhere.

entries.title: integration-test — testing a crate from the outside
entries.l1: An integration test exercises a crate the same way an OUTSIDE caller would — through its public API only, from a separate file, as if it were just another dependency. This catches bugs that a test living INSIDE the crate (with access to private internals) might miss, and it's where this codebase puts its biggest, most important checks: whole-artifact determinism, real-data law checks, and CLI behavior.
entries.l2:
Files under a crate's `tests/` directory (e.g. `server/atlas-graph/tests/determinism.rs`) are each compiled as their OWN separate crate that depends on the library under test through its public API — no `#[cfg(test)]` attribute needed, since the whole file only exists during `cargo test`.

Example: `server/atlas-graph/tests/determinism.rs` builds the real compiled graph artifact TWICE and asserts the two byte sequences are identical — testing the crate's actual observable output, not an internal function.

Newcomer mistake: putting a test that needs PRIVATE (non-`pub`) access into `tests/` — it won't compile, since integration tests can only see what the crate exposes publicly; that kind of test belongs inside the crate as a unit test instead.
entries.l3: `server/atlas-graph/tests/` holds this codebase's heaviest integration tests: `determinism.rs` (byte-identical rebuilds), `artifact_conformance.rs`, `attestation_exclusivity_real_data.rs`, `bible_containers_real_data.rs`, `chronology_laws.rs`, `exports_laws.rs`, `frontier_falsifiability.rs`, and others — many named 'real_data' because they build and check the ACTUAL committed dataset, not a synthetic fixture. `graph-types/tests/toolchain_pin.rs` and `server/atlas-cli/tests/cli.rs` are further examples, the latter literally shelling out to the compiled binary (see `Command-process`).

entries.title: unit-test — testing one piece from the inside
entries.l1: A unit test checks one small piece of behavior — usually a single function or type — with full access to a crate's PRIVATE internals, because it lives right inside the same file, just gated to only compile during testing. It's the quick, focused check: 'does THIS one function do the right thing', versus an integration test's 'does the whole crate behave correctly from the outside.'
entries.l3: `graph-types/src/graph.rs:514-515` (`#[cfg(test)] mod tests { use super::*; ... }`) runs this crate's own 'monad laws, the dual involution, the bijection witness, and temporal totality' checks (per `lib.rs:6-8`'s own description) directly against private graph internals. `graph-types/src/frontier.rs:589` has its own similarly-scoped test module. These sit alongside — not instead of — the crate's integration tests; `lib.rs:6-8` frames both together as the check that 'the design composes.'

entries.title: property-test — checking a rule against many random inputs
entries.l1: A property test doesn't check one hand-picked example — it checks that a RULE holds across hundreds of randomly generated inputs, and if it finds a failing case, it automatically shrinks it down to the smallest input that still breaks the rule. Instead of writing 'given these three specific dates, the result should be X', you write 'for ANY two dates in this range, this relationship should always hold' and let the tool hunt for counterexamples.
entries.l3: `server/atlas-core/src/history.rs:261,712,739`, `merge.rs`, `refs.rs`, `scene.rs`, `time.rs`, and `xrefs.rs` all `use proptest::prelude::*` and contain `proptest! { ... }` blocks — `atlas-core`'s `Cargo.toml` and `atlas-graph`'s `Cargo.toml` both list `proptest` as a dev-dependency. These are exactly the kind of algebraic law this codebase's culture prizes ('laws as tests'): merge associativity, chronology invariants, and reference-parsing round-trips checked against hundreds of generated cases rather than a handful of examples.

entries.title: bench — measuring speed, tracked over time
entries.l1: A benchmark measures how fast a piece of code runs, carefully enough to notice a real slowdown rather than just measurement noise — it runs the code many times, accounts for warm-up and variance, and reports a statistically sound number. This codebase keeps a PERMANENT benchmark harness specifically to catch performance regressions on real query workloads, not just correctness bugs.
entries.l3: `server/atlas-server/Cargo.toml:57,61` adds `criterion = "0.5"` as the 'permanent criterion regression harness'; `server/atlas-server/benches/queries.rs:65` (`fn load_real() -> (Arc<AtlasData>, Arc<GraphService>)`) loads the real committed data once and benchmarks actual query paths against it. `server/Cargo.toml:84,93,561` comments describe this as a 'permanent criterion/smoke-tier benchmark harness' and note it needs a release build to be meaningful — see `BENCHMARKS.md` at the server root for the tracked numbers themselves.

entries.title: workspace — several crates sharing one build
entries.l1: A Cargo workspace lets several crates share ONE dependency-resolution and ONE lock file, so they always build against consistent versions of shared dependencies instead of each crate potentially picking a different version of the same library. This project's `server/` directory is one workspace of five crates (`atlas-core`, `atlas-etl`, `atlas-server`, `atlas-graph`, `atlas-cli`); the sixth crate, `graph-types`, lives at the repo root and is pulled in as an ordinary path dependency rather than being a declared workspace member.
entries.l2:
`[workspace]` in a root `Cargo.toml` with a `members = [...]` list of crate directories; every member shares one `Cargo.lock` and one `target/` build output directory.

Example:
```
[workspace]
members = ["atlas-core", "atlas-etl", "atlas-server", "atlas-graph", "atlas-cli"]
resolver = "2"
```
Newcomer mistake: expecting every crate a workspace crate depends on to automatically become a workspace member — a plain path dependency (like `atlas-graph`'s dependency on `../../graph-types`) pulls a crate into the SAME lockfile/resolution without it needing to be listed in `members`.
entries.l3: `server/Cargo.toml:1-19` is unusually well-documented on exactly this point: `graph-types/` is deliberately NOT listed in `members` because Cargo requires every member to be hierarchically BELOW the workspace root, and `graph-types/` is a SIBLING of `server/`, not a descendant — moving it to satisfy that rule was judged a bigger deviation than working around it. `atlas-graph`'s plain `path = "../../graph-types"` dependency still pulls it into this ONE workspace's resolution and lockfile, and `cargo test -p atlas-graph-types` (run from `server/`) still reaches its 13 law tests even though it's a non-member — a 'standing counting procedure' comment right below (server/Cargo.toml) documents this two-command test-counting quirk for anyone running the full suite.

entries.title: Cargo.toml — a crate's manifest
entries.l1: `Cargo.toml` is a crate's ID card: its name, version, dependencies, and (for a workspace root) which sub-crates belong to it. It's the equivalent of `package.json` in Node or a `.csproj` in .NET — the one file Cargo (Rust's build tool) reads to know what to build and what it needs to build it.
entries.l2:
Key sections: `[package]` (name, version, edition), `[dependencies]` (what this crate needs), `[dev-dependencies]` (test/bench-only dependencies, like `proptest` or `criterion`), and `[workspace]` (only at a workspace root — see `workspace`).

Example:
```
[dependencies]
serde = { version = "1", features = ["derive"] }

[dev-dependencies]
proptest = "1"
criterion = "0.5"
```
Newcomer mistake: adding a test-only dependency under `[dependencies]` instead of `[dev-dependencies]` — that bloats the actual shipped/production build with a dependency only tests need.
entries.l3: `server/Cargo.toml` is this workspace's root manifest, holding both the `[workspace]` block (lines 1-19, with the extensive comment explaining why `graph-types` isn't a listed member) and dependency version notes elsewhere in the file (e.g. `criterion = "0.5"` at line 61 inside `atlas-server`'s own manifest). `graph-types/Cargo.toml` has had its OWN `[workspace]` marker deliberately removed (per `server/Cargo.toml`'s comment) so it doesn't compete with the real workspace root — a subtlety worth knowing if you ever wonder why a sibling crate's manifest looks unusually bare.

entries.title: build-script (build.rs) — code that runs before compiling
entries.l1: A Cargo build script (`build.rs`, at a crate's root, wired up via `build = "build.rs"` in `Cargo.toml`) is code that Cargo runs BEFORE compiling the rest of the crate — used for things like generating code, compiling a bundled C library, or emitting extra compiler flags. This codebase doesn't use one anywhere.
entries.l3: No `Cargo.toml` in this workspace declares a `build = "..."` entry (checked across `server/*/Cargo.toml` and `graph-types/Cargo.toml`), so no crate here has an actual Cargo build script. `server/atlas-graph/src/build.rs` is easy to mistake for one by name alone — it's a regular source module holding the graph-building pipeline's orchestration code, compiled as ordinary crate code, not run specially by Cargo before compilation.

entries.title: sort-determinism — same input, same bytes, every time
entries.l1: This project has a hard rule: build the same graph from the same source files twice, and you must get byte-for-byte IDENTICAL output both times — same order, same everything. That matters because the compiled graph gets content-hashed (see `content-hash`), and a hash is only a trustworthy fingerprint if equal inputs always produce equal bytes. The historical bug this rule guards against: using `HashMap` (whose iteration order is randomized per process) to write files meant that running the SAME build twice could produce two different-looking (but equally correct) files — which silently broke that trust.
entries.l2:
The fix, applied throughout: every collection whose contents end up serialized uses `BTreeMap`/`BTreeSet` (which always iterate in sorted order) or a plain `Vec` built by iterating deterministically-ordered sources — never a `HashMap` for anything that gets written out.

Example: `server/atlas-graph/tests/determinism.rs` builds the graph artifact twice and asserts `assert_eq!(bytes_one, bytes_two)`.

Newcomer mistake: assuming 'the values are the same' is enough — this codebase's own tests go further and compare raw BYTES, since two structurally-equal-but-differently-ORDERED outputs would pass a naive equality check while still failing a byte comparison (and producing a different hash).
entries.l3: `server/atlas-graph/tests/determinism.rs:1-19` documents the history directly: the old `verses-kjv.json`/`cross-refs.json` writers were `HashMap`-keyed and produced non-deterministic byte layouts; both files and their writers were deleted, and every row table `artifact.rs`'s `dump` now writes is sourced from `graph-types::graph::Graph`'s `Vec`/`BTreeMap` fields (`graph-types/src/graph.rs:27`), never a `HashMap`, built from sorted-by-filename curated source lists. The test itself (determinism.rs) is deliberately STRONGER than comparing version roots or `assert_answers_match`: it compares the entire dumped byte stream, catching ordering bugs a semantic-equality check would miss.

entries.title: content-hash — an id derived from the thing itself
entries.l1: Instead of handing out arbitrary, incrementing ids (1, 2, 3, ...), this project derives an id FROM the content itself — hash the thing's own canonical bytes, and that hash IS its id. The payoff: two things with identical content always get the identical id, automatically, with no coordination needed, and an id is 'self-verifying' — you can always recompute it from the content and check nothing's been silently altered. It's the same principle git commit hashes use.
entries.l3: `graph-types/src/id.rs:161-181` is the whole mechanism: `ContentHash(pub u64)` (id.rs:164), `Pid { kind: PositionKind, hash: ContentHash }` (id.rs:167-170), and the `ContentAddressed` trait's default `pid()` method (id.rs:174-182) computing `hash(canonical_bytes(derive(pid))) == pid` — a law stated directly in the comment above it (id.rs:172-173). `graph-types/src/store.rs:32` calls this 'the content-addressed store law — the canonical bytes of derive.' `graph-types/src/lib.rs:11` discloses the current hash is 'a 64-bit std hash (production: a real multihash)' — a deliberate, disclosed simplification, not an oversight.

entries.title: interning — one shared copy instead of many duplicates
entries.l1: Interning means: when the same piece of text (or value) shows up many times, store it ONCE and hand out cheap references to that one copy, instead of duplicating the full text every time it's needed — like a library keeping one copy of a book and lending it out, instead of printing a fresh copy for every borrower. This codebase names its id-backing type `Interned` to signal that intent, but — DISCLOSED directly in the crate's own doc comment — it's currently just a plain `String`, with no actual deduplication pool behind it yet.
entries.l2:
A real interner typically maps each distinct string to a small integer or handle, so equal strings become equal (and cheap-to-compare) handles instead of separately-allocated, separately-compared text.

Example (what exists today, not a real interner):
```
/// Skeleton stand-in for an interner handle.
pub type Interned = String;
```
Newcomer mistake: assuming `Interned` implies deduplication or cheap equality checks somewhere in this codebase today — it doesn't yet; comparing two `Interned` values currently means a full string comparison, exactly as it would for two plain `String`s, because that's literally what it is.
entries.l3: `graph-types/src/id.rs:7-8` (`/// Skeleton stand-in for an interner handle.` `pub type Interned = String;`) is the entire current implementation — a type alias, not a real interning pool (see `type-alias`). `graph-types/src/lib.rs:10-12`'s own top-level doc comment lists this among its 'deliberate, documented simplifications (none change shapes)': 'Interned is a String; ... tables are Vecs' — meaning a future swap to a real interner is anticipated to change performance characteristics only, not any type's public shape. Every id type built on `Interned` (`NodeId<K>`, `EdgeId`, `ProvenanceId`) would benefit from real interning without any of their own code changing.

entries.title: blazor-component — a self-contained piece of UI
entries.l1: A Blazor component is a reusable piece of the page — its own markup, its own logic, its own state — that you can drop into other pages like a custom HTML tag. The reader's verse card, the map's popover, the time slider: each is its own component, written once and reused everywhere it's needed, so a fix to how a popover behaves happens in one file instead of copy-pasted markup scattered across every page that shows one.
entries.l3: This codebase's components live under `client/Components/`, `client/Pages/`, `client/Views/`, and `client/Layout/` — e.g. `ArrowNav.razor`, `CompositionSplit.razor`, `ExplorerPopover.razor`, `CatechismList.razor`. `CompositionSplit.razor:281,317` shows a component both consuming an `EventCallback` parameter and exposing its own (`OnFractionCommitted`). Cross-component shared state that ISN'T naturally parent-to-child (like the split-view study layout) goes through an injected service instead (see `state-service`) — `client/Program.cs`'s comments explain this choice directly for `ViewStateService`.

entries.title: razor — HTML and C# in one file
entries.l1: Razor is the templating syntax that lets you write ordinary HTML and drop into C# mid-markup with an `@` sign — no separate templating language to learn, just HTML with an escape hatch into real code. `@if (loading) { <Spinner /> }` reads almost like plain HTML with a conditional woven in, because that's essentially what it is.
entries.l3: Every `.razor` file across `client/Components/`, `client/Pages/`, `client/Views/`, and `client/Layout/` is razor syntax — the component system (see `blazor-component`) IS razor: markup plus an `@code` block. `client/App.razor` is the root component that bootstraps routing for the whole single-page app.

entries.title: dependency-injection — services handed to you, not looked up
entries.l1: Dependency injection means a component or service declares 'I need one of these' and the framework hands it the right instance automatically, rather than the component going and constructing (or globally looking up) it itself. It's what lets `AtlasClient` (the thing that talks to the server) be built ONCE at startup and then handed to every component or service that needs it, without each one knowing how to construct one itself.
entries.l2:
Registered once in `Program.cs` (`builder.Services.AddSingleton(...)`, `AddScoped(...)`), then requested via `@inject TypeName Name` in a razor component or a constructor parameter in a plain C# class.

Example:
```
builder.Services.AddSingleton<IExplorableClient>(_ => new GraphExplorableClient(new HttpClient { ... }));
```
```
@inject IExplorableClient Client
```
Newcomer mistake: registering something as `AddScoped` out of habit (copied from ASP.NET Core server conventions) in a Blazor WASM app — WASM has no per-request scope the way a server does; `AddSingleton` is usually the right choice there, as this codebase's own `Program.cs` comment on `ViewStateService` explains directly.
entries.l3: `client/Program.cs:15-30` registers `HttpClient`, `AtlasClient`, and `IExplorableClient` (backed by `GraphExplorableClient`) as singletons, with a comment (lines 24-27) explaining the interface is depended on everywhere rather than the concrete `GraphExplorableClient` type directly — the standard DI principle of depending on an abstraction. `client/Program.cs`'s later comment about `ViewStateService` explains WHY `AddSingleton` (not `AddScoped`) is the deliberately correct choice specifically in Blazor WASM.

entries.title: wasm — running .NET code in the browser
entries.l1: WebAssembly (WASM) is a way to run compiled code directly in the browser at near-native speed, alongside (or instead of) JavaScript. Blazor WebAssembly compiles the C# client app to WASM and ships it to the browser, so the reader and the map run as REAL .NET code on your machine — no round trip to a server for every click — rather than a server rendering pages and sending HTML down each time.
entries.l2:
`WebAssemblyHostBuilder.CreateDefault(args)` bootstraps a Blazor WASM app in `Program.cs`; the compiled app (C#, the .NET runtime, and your code) downloads once and then runs entirely client-side, calling the server only for actual data (via `HttpClient`).

Example:
```
var builder = WebAssemblyHostBuilder.CreateDefault(args);
builder.RootComponents.Add<App>("#app");
```
Newcomer mistake: assuming WASM means 'just like a normal desktop app' with unrestricted access to the machine — a WASM app runs sandboxed inside the browser, so anything touching the DOM, local files, or browser APIs goes through JS interop (see `js-interop`) rather than direct OS calls.
entries.l3: `client/Program.cs:11-13` (`WebAssemblyHostBuilder.CreateDefault(args); builder.RootComponents.Add<App>("#app");`) is this app's WASM entry point. `client/LocalStore.cs:19-23`'s own doc comment notes a WASM-specific consequence directly: Blazor WASM's DI-registered `IJSRuntime` always implements `IJSInProcessRuntime` because there's no network hop to a separate browser process the way Blazor SERVER has — so every JS interop call here can be synchronous, no `Task`/`await` needed for what would otherwise be a network round trip in Blazor Server.

entries.title: js-interop — C# calling JavaScript, and back
entries.l1: JS interop is the bridge that lets C# code call JavaScript functions (for things only the browser can do, like drawing the Leaflet map) and lets JavaScript call BACK into C# (like reporting 'the user hovered over this place marker'). The map itself is JavaScript (Leaflet); the C# side drives it and listens to it through this bridge, rather than reimplementing map rendering in C#.
entries.l3: `client/MapInterop.cs:1-20` defines `IMapEvents`, the interface `map.js`'s `wireEvents`/`ArrowLayer` call back into C# through, implemented by `World.razor`; `MapEventsSink` (referenced at MapInterop.cs:12) is the actual JS-callable bridge object. `client/LocalStore.cs:18-23` explains the reverse direction (C# calling into JS for `localStorage`), and its own doc comment is explicit that Blazor WASM's `IJSRuntime` always implements `IJSInProcessRuntime`, making these calls plain synchronous method calls rather than async ones.

entries.title: record — a value defined by its data
entries.l1: A `record` is a C# type built for VALUES rather than identity — two records with the same field values are automatically considered equal, and printing one automatically shows all its fields, without you writing that comparison or printing code by hand. It's the natural fit for the small, immutable data shapes this app passes around: a Scene, a TimeRange, a Focus — things defined entirely by what they contain, not by which specific instance you're holding.
entries.l2:
`public record Name(Type Field1, Type Field2);` gives you a constructor, equality, `ToString()`, and (for a positional record) property getters, all generated. `with` expressions create a modified copy: `var updated = original with { Field1 = newValue };`.

Example:
```
public sealed record TimeRangeDto(int FromYear, int ToYear);
```
Newcomer mistake: mutating a record's properties in place expecting the usual reference-type sharing semantics of a `class` — records are meant to be treated as immutable snapshots; the idiomatic way to 'change' one is `with { ... }`, producing a NEW record rather than modifying the original in place.
entries.l3: `client/Dtos.cs:13,26,28` (`Scene`, `TimeRangeDto`, `ScenePlace`) defines the client's wire-facing data shapes as records. `client/Contracts/Focus.cs:18` and `Interactions.cs:52` use records for in-app value types (`Focus`, `TimingDiscipline`). `client/MapInterop.cs:158` and `SavedExplorationsService.cs:82,90` use `with` expressions (`s with { Places = ... }`, `i with { Name = name }`) to produce modified copies via LINQ's `.Select()` — the idiomatic 'immutable update' pattern this codebase leans on throughout its client-side state handling.

entries.title: async Task — C#'s pausable operations
entries.l1: `async`/`Task` is C#'s version of the same idea Rust's `async`/`await` covers: a method that can pause while waiting on something slow (a network call to the server) without blocking the whole browser tab. Every call from the client out to the atlas server — fetching a scene, a chapter, a place's history — is one of these, so the UI stays responsive while waiting for a response.
entries.l3: `client/AtlasClient.cs:86,99,116,163,189` (`SceneTime`, `SceneScripture`, `Chapter`, `PlaceHistory`, `Xrefs`) are all `async Task<T>` methods wrapping HTTP calls to the atlas server. This mirrors the server side's own `async fn` axum handlers (see `async-await`) — the same asynchronous-request idiom on both ends of the wire, just in two different languages.

entries.title: LINQ — querying collections like a sentence
entries.l1: LINQ lets you filter, transform, and search collections with readable, chainable operations — `.Where(...)`, `.Select(...)`, `.FirstOrDefault(...)` — instead of hand-written loops with manual index bookkeeping. It reads close to a sentence: 'take these places, where the name matches, and give me the first one.'
entries.l2:
Method-syntax LINQ (the style used throughout this codebase): `collection.Where(predicate).Select(transform).ToList()`. Common terminal operations: `.FirstOrDefault()`, `.Any()`, `.OrderBy()`, `.ToList()`.

Example:
```
var forMap = s with { Places = s.Places.Select(p => p with { Name = p.DisplayName }).ToList() };
```
Newcomer mistake: calling `.ToList()` (or another eager operation) too early in a chain, then filtering afterward — like Rust's iterators, LINQ is LAZY until a terminal operation runs, so materializing early can waste work building a list you're about to filter down anyway.
entries.l3: `client/MapInterop.cs:158` and `client/SavedExplorationsService.cs:82,90` use `.Select()`/`.Where()` with `with` expressions (see `record`) for immutable-style updates to lists of records. `client/Explore/BookNode.cs:38` (`toc.FirstOrDefault(b => b.Code == _bookCode)`) and `client/Explore/ExplorationDescriptor.cs:141-142` (`.Where(v => v.Verse >= span.FromVerse && v.Verse <= span.ToVerse).Select(v => v.Text)`) use LINQ for lookup and text-extraction logic against the client's exploration/reader data.

entries.title: EventCallback — a component's way of speaking to its parent
entries.l1: An `EventCallback` is how a child component tells its PARENT 'something happened here' — like a button reporting 'I was clicked' up to whoever placed it, without the button needing to know what the parent will actually do about it. Data flows DOWN from parent to child via parameters; events flow back UP via `EventCallback`, keeping the direction of communication consistent and predictable.
entries.l2:
`[Parameter] public EventCallback<T> OnSomething { get; set; }` on the child; the parent passes a method: `<Child OnSomething="HandleIt" />`; the child invokes it with `await OnSomething.InvokeAsync(value)`.

Example:
```
[Parameter, EditorRequired] public EventCallback<IExplorable> OnExplore { get; set; }
```
Newcomer mistake: using a plain C# `Action`/`Func` delegate instead of `EventCallback` for a component parameter — `EventCallback` integrates with Blazor's rendering system (it knows to trigger a re-render after being invoked); a raw delegate doesn't, unless the component that OWNS the underlying state handles re-rendering itself, which is exactly the deliberate exception `CompositionSplit.razor`'s own comment calls out.
entries.l3: `client/Components/ArrowNav.razor:360` and `CatechismList.razor:46` both declare `[Parameter, EditorRequired] public EventCallback<IExplorable> OnExplore { get; set; }` — the shared way any explorable-node component reports 'the user picked this' upward. `CompositionSplit.razor:281,317,342` shows both an `EventCallback.Factory.Create(this, RequestCloseAsync)` construction and a deliberate exception: a plain `Action` (not `EventCallback`) for `ViewArrangementAtom.Changed`, with a comment explaining that field is owned elsewhere and doesn't need Blazor's own re-render hook.

entries.title: CascadingParameter — passing data down many levels at once
entries.l1: A cascading parameter is a way to make a value available to every DESCENDANT component in a tree, without threading it explicitly through every single component in between as an ordinary parameter — like a public address announcement reaching everyone in a building at once, rather than a note passed hand-to-hand down every floor. Not used anywhere in this codebase's Rust... rather, its C# client.
entries.l2:
`<CascadingValue Value="@someValue"><ChildContent/></CascadingValue>` in a parent makes `someValue` available to any descendant that declares `[CascadingParameter] public T Value { get; set; }`, at ANY nesting depth, without every intermediate component needing to know about or re-pass it.

Example (illustrative, not from this repo):
```
<CascadingValue Value="@currentTheme">
    <PageBody />
</CascadingValue>
```
Newcomer mistake: reaching for a cascading parameter for something only ONE direct child needs — that's simpler and more explicit as an ordinary `[Parameter]`; cascading values are for data genuinely needed by an unpredictable, deep set of descendants.
entries.l3: A search across every `.razor` and `.cs` file in `client/` found no `CascadingValue`/`CascadingParameter` usage at all. Where this codebase needs to share context across a subtree (e.g. split-view state), it instead passes an explicit typed value — `CompositionSplitContext` (`client/Components/CompositionSplitContext.cs:42`, a plain `record`) — directly as a `[Parameter]`, or reaches for an injected singleton service (see `state-service`) when the sharing crosses unrelated parts of the component tree entirely rather than a strict parent-descendant chain.

entries.title: state-service — shared state that outlives any one component
entries.l1: A state service is a plain C# class, registered once with dependency injection, that holds state meant to be shared across UNRELATED parts of the app — the current view arrangement, saved explorations, selection state — the way a single shared notebook works better than each component keeping its own private copy and hoping they stay in sync. Components inject it and read/write it directly, and can subscribe to a 'changed' event to re-render when it updates.
entries.l3: `client/ViewStateService.cs`, `client/SavedExplorationsService.cs`, and `client/LocalStore.cs`'s two consumers together form this codebase's state-service layer. `client/LocalStore.cs:6-16`'s own doc comment describes the idiom directly: 'restore on init, synced continuously at the point state actually changes, never captured lazily', and explicitly contrasts `ViewStateService`'s in-memory-only Map/Reader halves (never persisted) against the newer, genuinely durable localStorage-backed stores it now supports.

entries.title: localStorage — the browser's own small file cabinet
entries.l1: `localStorage` is a small key-value storage area the browser keeps for each website, surviving page reloads and browser restarts — like a filing cabinet built into the browser itself. This app uses it to remember things across visits: saved explorations, view preferences — anything that should still be there next time you open the app, without needing a server account.
entries.l3: `client/LocalStore.cs:1-23` is the shared primitive `SavedExplorationsService` and `SelectionTrayService` both build on — a plain, camelCase JSON document per key, explicitly NOT the same snake_case convention `Wire.cs` uses for server communication (LocalStore.cs:14-16 notes this distinction directly: this is a client-local document, never a wire DTO). Its own comment explains why every read/write here can be a synchronous call rather than async: Blazor WASM's `IJSRuntime` is always also an `IJSInProcessRuntime` (see `wasm`), unlike Blazor Server.

entries.title: HttpClient — calling the server
entries.l1: `HttpClient` is the standard .NET tool for making web requests — it's how the Blazor client actually talks to the Rust atlas server, fetching scenes, chapters, place histories, and cross-references over HTTP. One `HttpClient`, configured once with the server's base address, gets reused for every request rather than creating a fresh connection setup each time.
entries.l3: `client/Program.cs:15-30` registers TWO separate `HttpClient` instances deliberately: one for `AtlasClient`, one for `GraphExplorableClient` — a comment there explains the separation is intentional, not an oversight (see that file's own header comment for why). `client/AtlasClient.cs:24,62` (`private readonly HttpClient _http; public AtlasClient(HttpClient http) { ... }`) receives its client via constructor injection rather than constructing one itself, keeping the class testable and its network configuration centralized in `Program.cs`.

entries.title: System.Text.Json — .NET's built-in JSON library
entries.l1: `System.Text.Json` is the standard, built-in way .NET code converts between C# objects and JSON text — the C# counterpart to Rust's `serde`. It's what turns the server's JSON response into a usable `Scene` object in C#, and what would turn a C# object back into JSON to send somewhere, all without a third-party dependency.
entries.l2:
`JsonSerializer.Serialize(value)` / `JsonSerializer.Deserialize<T>(json)`; `JsonSerializerOptions` configures details like naming conventions (`camelCase` vs `PascalCase`) shared consistently across every call site.

Example:
```
using System.Text.Json;

public static readonly JsonSerializerOptions Options = new() { /* shared settings */ };
```
Newcomer mistake: constructing a fresh `JsonSerializerOptions` at every call site instead of sharing one configured instance — that risks subtly inconsistent serialization behavior (naming, casing) between different parts of the app talking to the same server.
entries.l3: `client/Wire.cs:1,15` defines one shared `JsonSerializerOptions Options` for the whole client, with a header comment establishing its own snake_case convention specifically for talking to the atlas server (contrasted directly against `LocalStore.cs`'s camelCase, client-local convention — see `localStorage`). `AtlasClient.cs`'s `GetFromJsonAsync<T>` calls rely on this same options/DTO convention for every server response the client deserializes.

entries.title: xunit — the C# test framework used here
entries.l1: xUnit is the test framework this project's C# tests run on — the counterpart to Rust's built-in `#[test]`. A test method marked `[Fact]` runs once; `[Theory]` with `[InlineData(...)]` runs the same test body against several different inputs, similar in spirit to a lightweight version of Rust's property tests but with explicit, hand-picked cases rather than randomly generated ones.
entries.l3: `client.Tests/` holds this codebase's C# unit tests — files like `AcctCoalesceTests.cs`, `AqcContractTests.cs`, `ArrowNavTests.cs`, `AsyncMemoConformanceTests.cs`, `AsyncMemoTests.cs` all use xunit's `[Fact]`/`[Theory]` attributes (per the project's `PackageReference Include="xunit"` in its `.csproj`). These tests exercise client-side LOGIC classes (services, DTO handling, LINQ-based helpers) directly, in-process, without needing a browser or a rendering harness.

entries.title: bUnit — testing Blazor components directly
entries.l1: bUnit is a testing library specifically for rendering Blazor components in a test, without a real browser, so you can assert on the rendered markup or simulate a click and check what happens — a Blazor-specific alternative to a full end-to-end browser test. This codebase's own `client.Tests` project does NOT use it: no `bUnit`/`TestContext` reference was found anywhere.
entries.l3: `client.Tests/*.csproj` lists only `xunit`, `xunit.runner.visualstudio`, `Microsoft.NET.Test.Sdk`, and `coverlet.collector` as test-related packages — no `bunit` package reference anywhere. This means `client.Tests` covers plain C# classes and services (see `xunit`) directly, while actual rendered-component and full-page behavior is instead covered by the Playwright end-to-end suite under `tests/ux/` (see `Playwright`) and the Gherkin/Reqnroll contract tests under `client.ContractTests/` (see `Reqnroll`) — two different layers filling the gap a bUnit suite would otherwise cover.

entries.title: Reqnroll — running Gherkin scenarios as C# tests
entries.l1: Reqnroll is the tool that takes a plain-English Gherkin scenario (see `Gherkin`) — 'When I GET /api/eras, Then the consumed projection equals fixture X' — and actually RUNS it as a real test, by matching each line to a C# 'step definition' method that performs that action. It's the glue between a human-readable feature description and executable test code.
entries.l2:
A `.feature` file (Gherkin) describes scenarios in plain English; a `[Binding]`-attributed C# class with `[When("...")]`/`[Then("...")]` methods (matched by regex or a Cucumber-expression) implements each step.

Example:
```
[When("I GET {string}")]
public async Task WhenIGet(string path) { /* perform the HTTP call */ }
```
Newcomer mistake: writing step definitions so specific to ONE scenario's wording that they can't be reused by the next scenario — the value of Gherkin/Reqnroll comes from a small vocabulary of steps being reused across many scenarios; near-duplicate steps mean the vocabulary is growing instead of being reused.
entries.l3: `contracts/atlas-edge/*.feature` (e.g. `eras.feature`, `events.feature`, `land-mask.feature`, `landmarks.feature`, `narratives.feature`) are the Gherkin scenario files. `client.ContractTests/Steps/AqcSteps.cs` and `CorpusCountTests.cs` are the Reqnroll step-definition/binding code that actually executes them, per the `Reqnroll`/`Reqnroll.xUnit.ReqnrollPlugin` packages referenced in `client.ContractTests`'s build output. This is this codebase's API-contract layer: each `.feature` file's vocabulary of 'projections' is checked against the real server's actual JSON responses.

entries.title: Playwright — driving a real browser for tests
entries.l1: Playwright automates an actual browser — clicking, typing, navigating — so a test can verify the app behaves correctly the way a real person using it would, rather than testing isolated pieces of logic. This project's end-to-end tests (`tests/ux/`) use it to check things like: does hovering a cross-reference marker actually open the right popover, anchored correctly, in a real rendered page.
entries.l3: `tests/ux/` holds this codebase's whole Playwright suite: `accounts-and-mentions.spec.ts`, `api-exhaustive.spec.ts`, `api-place-history.spec.ts`, `api-reader.spec.ts`, `api-scene.spec.ts`, `frontier-matrix.spec.ts`, and many more — end-to-end checks against the running app, some purely API-level (per `client/FeatureFlags.cs`'s own comment mentioning `tests/ux/reader-xref-superscripts.spec.ts` covering the reader's cross-reference-superscript feature directly).

entries.title: fast-check — property-based testing for TypeScript/JS
entries.l1: fast-check is JavaScript/TypeScript's version of the same idea as Rust's `proptest`: instead of one hand-picked example, it generates hundreds of random inputs and checks that a RULE holds across all of them, shrinking any failure down to the smallest input that still breaks it. This codebase uses it for math-heavy, pure-logic checks — like verifying the sphere/vector coordinate conversion is correct for ANY latitude/longitude, not just a few chosen test points.
entries.l2:
`import fc from 'fast-check'; fc.assert(fc.property(fc.double({ min: ..., max: ... }), (x) => { /* property that must hold */ }));` — `fc.double`/`fc.integer`/etc. describe the RANGE of random values to generate.

Example:
```
import fc from 'fast-check';

const lat = () => fc.double({ min: -Math.PI / 2 + EPS_POLE, max: Math.PI / 2 - EPS_POLE, noNaN: true });
```
Newcomer mistake: forgetting `noNaN: true` (or an equivalent constraint) when generating floating-point inputs for geometry/math code — NaN inputs can trigger unrelated failures that have nothing to do with the actual property being tested, muddying the results.
entries.l3: `tests/ux/geo.spec.ts:2,8-9,30-44` is this codebase's clearest example: a comment there explicitly frames it as 'a pure-node fast-check spec that never opens a browser is fine and fast', generating latitude/longitude/bearing/fraction values (`fc.double({...})`) to check the sphere-to-vector coordinate conversion functions in `client/wwwroot/js/geo.js` (see `ES-module`) hold their mathematical properties for any valid input, not just a handful of hand-picked angles.

entries.title: Gherkin — plain-English test scenarios
entries.l1: Gherkin is a structured, plain-English way of writing test scenarios so a non-programmer can read (and even write) them: 'Given ..., When ..., Then ...' — a shared vocabulary between what the app is supposed to do and the tests that check it does it. This project uses it to describe its API contract in language close to the domain ('the consumed projection eras equals fixture X') rather than raw HTTP assertions.
entries.l2:
A `.feature` file: `Feature: name` followed by one or more `Scenario:` blocks, each a sequence of `Given`/`When`/`Then`/`And` lines. A tool like Reqnroll (see `Reqnroll`) matches each line to real test code that executes it.

Example:
```
Scenario: the whole era table, as we consume it
  When I GET /api/eras
  Then the consumed projection eras equals fixture "eras-consumed"
```
Newcomer mistake: writing Gherkin steps that describe IMPLEMENTATION details ('When I call the internal parse_eras function') instead of observable BEHAVIOR ('When I GET /api/eras') — Gherkin's whole value is describing behavior a non-programmer stakeholder could verify, which implementation-level steps defeat.
entries.l3: `contracts/atlas-edge/*.feature` — `eras.feature`, `events.feature`, `land-mask.feature`, `landmarks.feature`, `narratives.feature` — are this codebase's Gherkin contract specifications. `eras.feature:1-11` is a representative example: its header prose explains WHAT the underlying `parse_eras` function reads (four fields per era) before its `Scenario:` block states the observable HTTP behavior being verified, with a shared `Vocabulary:` table (era.feature:6-7) defining the fixed set of valid 'projection' names reused across scenarios.

entries.title: Leaflet — the map library rendering /world
entries.l1: Leaflet is the JavaScript library that actually draws the interactive map — panning, zooming, markers, custom layers — that the `/world` page's borders and time slider sit on top of. Blazor doesn't render maps itself; the C# side drives Leaflet through JS interop (see `js-interop`), telling it what to draw and listening for what the user does on it.
entries.l2:
A Leaflet map is created with `L.map('elementId')`, then layers (tile layers, markers, polygons for borders) are added to it; custom behavior (like this project's era-morph border animation) is built as Leaflet plugins/layers in plain JS.

Example (illustrative, Leaflet's own API):
```
const map = L.map('map').setView([31.8, 35.2], 6);
L.marker([31.78, 35.23]).addTo(map);
```
Newcomer mistake: expecting to control Leaflet directly from C# component code the way you'd control a native Blazor component — Leaflet lives entirely in JS; every interaction crosses the JS-interop boundary (see `js-interop`) rather than being a normal C# method call.
entries.l3: `client/wwwroot/vendor/leaflet/leaflet.js` and `leaflet.css` are the vendored library; `client/wwwroot/js/map.js` is this project's own driving code on top of it — wiring event handlers (`wireEvents`, `ArrowLayer`, per `MapInterop.cs`'s own comment), rendering place markers, and (per `map.js:3554-3563`'s own comment) currently rendering border-morph animation via Leaflet/SVG rather than WebGL, with WebGL noted there as a possible future 'swap seam' rather than something implemented today — see `WebGL`.

entries.title: SVG — drawing shapes with markup, not pixels
entries.l1: SVG (Scalable Vector Graphics) describes shapes — lines, curves, borders — as MATH (points and paths) rather than a grid of colored pixels, so it stays crisp at any zoom level. This project's map borders and legend icons are drawn this way, which is why zooming into a polity's border on the map doesn't blur or pixelate the way a zoomed bitmap image would.
entries.l2:
Written as XML-like markup (`<svg><path d="..."/></svg>`) either inline in HTML or generated dynamically from JavaScript via `document.createElementNS(...)` (the DOM API for creating namespaced elements like SVG, which plain `createElement` can't produce correctly).

Example:
```
<svg viewBox="0 0 100 100">
  <path d="M10 10 L90 90" stroke="black" />
</svg>
```
Newcomer mistake: trying to create an SVG element with plain `document.createElement('path')` — SVG elements need the NAMESPACED `createElementNS('http://www.w3.org/2000/svg', 'path')` form, or the browser won't render them correctly as SVG at all.
entries.l3: `client/wwwroot/js/map.js` and Leaflet itself (`client/wwwroot/vendor/leaflet/leaflet.js`) use SVG for rendering vector shapes on the map — Leaflet's default vector renderer is SVG-based. `client/Components/Legend.razor` uses inline SVG markup for legend iconography directly in razor markup (mixing HTML and SVG tags, since SVG is valid inside HTML). The border-morph animation work (see `WebGL`) currently renders through this same SVG/Leaflet path rather than a lower-level GPU approach.

entries.title: WebGL — drawing with the GPU directly
entries.l1: WebGL lets JavaScript draw graphics using the computer's GPU directly, which is dramatically faster than SVG or plain HTML/CSS for complex, frequently-changing visuals — think smoothly animating many shapes at once rather than a static or slowly-changing drawing. This project doesn't use it today; its border-morph animation is explicitly called out in a code comment as a candidate for a FUTURE move to WebGL, not something currently implemented.
entries.l2:
Accessed via `canvas.getContext('webgl')` (or `'webgl2'`), then drawing happens through low-level graphics primitives (vertex buffers, shaders) rather than DOM elements — a much lower-level, more verbose API than SVG or Canvas 2D, in exchange for far higher performance at scale.

Example (illustrative, not from this repo):
```
const gl = canvas.getContext('webgl');
// upload vertex data, compile shaders, draw
```
Newcomer mistake: assuming 'we mention WebGL in a comment' means it's implemented — check the actual rendering code; a documented future direction is not the same as current behavior, which is exactly the case here.
entries.l3: `client/wwwroot/js/map.js:3554,3563` explicitly discusses 'the GPU/WebGL swap seam' and notes 'a WebGL evaluator would instead upload posA/posB per-vertex attribute[s]' for the border-morph animation — framed as a possible FUTURE optimization for the vector-based border interpolation (see the related `border-morph-vector-idea` project memory), not code that exists yet. Today, that animation renders through Leaflet's SVG path instead (see `Leaflet`, `SVG`).

entries.title: ES-module — JavaScript's own import/export system
entries.l1: An ES module is a JavaScript file that explicitly declares what it exports (so other files can import exactly those pieces) and what it imports from elsewhere — the standard, built-in way JS files depend on each other, without needing a bundler or a global-namespace convention (like every function just living on `window`). It's the same organizing idea as Rust's `mod`/`pub use` or C#'s `using`, just JavaScript's native version.
entries.l3: `client/wwwroot/js/geo.js:36,53,87,98,103,110,114,118` exports its coordinate-conversion functions (`toVec`, `fromVec`, `dot`, `cross`, `norm`, etc.) as a small, pure, framework-agnostic module — its own header comment (geo.js:4-10) notes it deliberately has no Leaflet or DOM dependency specifically so it can be imported both from the browser (`map.js`/`border-morph.js`) AND from plain Node for its `tests/ux/geo.spec.ts` fast-check spec, with zero setup, purely because it's a standard ES module rather than something requiring a browser environment or bundler configuration.

entries.title: CSS — how the app looks
entries.l1: CSS (Cascading Style Sheets) is the language that controls how HTML actually looks — colors, spacing, layout, fonts — separate from the markup structure itself and separate from the C#/JS logic. This project's overall app styling and the vendored Leaflet map's own default styling both live as `.css` files loaded once for the whole app.
entries.l3: `client/wwwroot/css/app.css` is this project's main application stylesheet; `client/wwwroot/vendor/leaflet/leaflet.css` is the vendored map library's own required styling, loaded alongside it so Leaflet's markers, controls, and panes render correctly. Component-specific styling elsewhere in this codebase generally lives inline in razor markup or scoped alongside the relevant `.razor` file rather than in one monolithic sheet.
